speechtext:
Under the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada the statutes relating to the marketing of Newfoundland salt fish were to remain in effect for a period of five years from the date of union. Under this arrangement the exclusive right to market salt fish, including export to the mainland, was given to the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited. This was continued without change for five years.
In the spring of 1954 an extension of three years was granted to the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited, with the modification that export permits for wet salted fish were to be issued freely for movement to the Canadian mainland and the continental United States. This arrangement was extended on a temporary basis.
The exclusive right to export the products of a single province has no counterpart in the administration of the fisheries of any other province. However, it has been recognized by the government of Canada that a suitable period of time was desirable in which to effect a transfer to the normal practice of marketing. As nine years have now elapsed since union, one more year is considered ample for the completion of the transition. Therefore, the government has decided that the exclusive right of export held by the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited shall terminate on July 31, 1959.

When I adjourned the debate yesterday evening, I had mentioned the fact that we do not give our agricultural research services the leadership and scope we

should. I had also pointed out that in 1957 the United States had spent $50,000,000 on such services, an amount which has been found inadequate by several American commentators who have dealt with the matter.
Some time ago I read that no European country had done more than France, since the end of the last war, to apply specialization and scientific methods to the various aspects of its agriculture. We are told that the remarkable economic recovery of Europe has an intimate relationship with that research work.
Over the last few years, northern European countries not only have considerably increased their areas under wheat, barley or oats, but have found new consumer uses for their agricultural surpluses.
Those are the reasons for our surplus problems, and I suggest that, unless immediate development facilities are made available to our research services, a few years hence we will be unable to dispose of our surpluses.
When from time to time the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) tells us that Canada has sold or has given large quantities of our farm surpluses to underdeveloped countries, either on the basis of a long term loan or as a grant under the Colombo plan, we welcome the news. But, there again, it provides merely temporary relief to our difficulties.
In Pakistan and in India I had the opportunity to inspect huge dams which, in 10, 15 or 20 years, through irrigation of lands which are now marginal, will yield a large crop of grains, and it could be that, by that time, those countries will give us stiff competition on the world markets.
Therefore, through scientific research, we should find new uses for our farm products. Science is now finding the answer to the problem of the use of farm surpluses. Let us follow suit in this field. We already have a first-rate research bureau, and it is up to us to give it the necessary leadership.
Accordingly, we on this side of the house, feel that the government should immediately implement a vigorous program of scientific research, and if we were in power today, we would set up, starting this very year, a large scale research organization.
We also believe that our government experts and specialists should have much more frequent contacts and exchanges with
Supply-Agriculture
their counterparts abroad, so that the latest methods available be applied without delay.
We also believe that on a strictly federal-provincial basis, conferences should be frequently called with experts and specialists from the provincial governments so that all the provinces could have access to recent information and use it.
I do my best to keep abreast of problems which our farmers and producers have to face. I think our approach to those problems should be altogether different. Canadian agriculture should be reformed from top to bottom.
The Liberal party is a party of reform. At present, all it can do is to point out the facts to the government and make some suggestions as to policy. But the day will come when we shall put before the farmers and rural producers of our country a bold, original, new and revolutionary program of farm reform, and our friends from the western provinces certainly shall return to us much sooner than hon. gentlemen opposite think they will, and no doubt in far greater strength than they imagine.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I shall mention that I read with great interest the long list of election promises made by the Minister of Agriculture throughout the country during his last campaign. He has about promised everything, except that he ignored the most important field, that of research. This is an indication that he doesn't appreciate its real significance.
In any case we called his attention to this field, and during the next session, we shall not forget to ask about the progress, if any, made in this field.

Mr. Chairman, as they see me rise this morning, a number of hon. members may think I will bother to answer the speech delivered by the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). Let them have no worry on this account. I will certainly not give any publicity to a speech which is hardly worth it.
I am happy to have the opportunity of taking part in a debate on the work done by the Department of Agriculture.
In talking of Canadian agriculture, I know only too well that I shall be speaking of that sector of our population which constitutes the main element of stability in our economy, which offers the best talents that a nation can be endowed with, and whose right-minded philosophy and understanding

Supply-Agriculture
of things have always shown that it remains the country's main strength.
I have carefully read the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture when his estimates were brought down. With all due deference,
I must say that I was not greatly impressed by the minister's eloquence. And I believe that my impression is shared by the overwhelming majority of Canadian farmers who have read this speech.
As indicated on page 2074 of Hansard, this is what the minister said:
The farm situation has improved steadily in late 1957 and 1958, to a considerable extent I think since this government came into office and instituted new policies in connection with agriculture.
On the following page, the minister returned to the attack, in the following terms:
As I have said, I think a great deal of the improvement has been as the result of policies followed by this government, including the introduction of the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
The minister thinks highly of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. I would like to have the time to show in detail that, up to now, the application of this act is far from having provided the farmers with the great advantages which the minister boasts of; but I shall touch briefly on this during my remarks. For the moment I will simply say that for all the minister's bragging, the few minor successes which he has achieved are due, in the overwhelming majority of cases, to the implementation of acts passed by the Liberal government, and to the fulfilment of the program which the Liberals launched when they were in office.
Mr. Chairman, in speaking of Canadian agriculture, some facts must be analysed if one is to grasp the complexity of the country's agricultural problems.
Thus, out of 623,000 farms in Canada, we find that the average area of farms in Newfoundland, in 1951, was 23 acres, whereas it was 527 acres in Alberta, and 550 in Saskatchewan.
Then there is the problem of our farms on the southern and south-eastern coasts of Nova Scotia, of Cape Breton, and of the centre and the northeast of New Brunswick, as well as the farms of the Gaspe district and northern Quebec and Ontario, which provide a meagre livelihood for their owners.
There is a world of difference between many of these farmers who sell $500 worth of produce and who have to eke out a living by taking on outside work and the farmers on the outskirts of large cities where milk is sold at $4 per cwt., or the western farmers who own a half section or a full section of land.
The same difference exists between the young farmer-even if he has obtained a farm loan-who starts off in northern Quebec and Ontario and the one who has a flock of
100,000	to 200,000 fowl and who is near thickly populated centres which offer a ready market for his produce.
The farmers do, however, still have one thing in common. That is the interest they have in the income they obtain from their work, and their attitude of looking upon their work as a professional calling rather than a way of life.
With the ever increasing commercialization of agriculture, a whole array of problems arise which affect both domestic and foreign markets.
Several factors bring their influence to bear on the domestic markets, and the prices of agricultural products depend on such factors as the weather, diseases of plants and livestock, outbreaks of contagious diseases and other factors, resulting in unpredictable fluctuations in the rythm of production and the prices of some foodstuffs.
While these factors are not the only ones which affect the income of farmers, the fact remains that, unlike his counterpart in industry, the farmer does not have a steady income year in and year out.
The impact of foreign markets is another factor which has a great deal of influence upon stability in agriculture and the country's economy as a whole. Actually, Canada exports a wide range of agricultural products, including cereals, potatoes, grass seeds, tobacco, apples and livestock products consisting almost exclusively of beef, pork, bacon and cheese. Of all the products, the most important is wheat. For quite some time, Canada has been exporting 60 per cent of her overall production, i.e. 300 million bushels annually.
It is easy to understand the difficult position in which a country finds itself, in the face of ever increasing competition from other countries which want to corner the world market

sometimes in a way which seems to us like hitting below the belt.
But these are not the matters I intend to deal with today, my aim is rather to deal with the agricultural program which we shall have to work out to meet the ever-growing need for food products.
These needs are unequivocally illustrated in the report on an inquiry into the progress and the prospect of agriculture in Canada.

This shows that in the future, the available individual income will have risen by an average of approximately 18 per cent by 1965, and 70 per cent by 1980. This increased buying power will be accompanied by a population increase resulting from the birth rate and controlled immigration. We see from the report that the index of the volume of over-all production should rise to 232, based on an index of 100 for the period 1935-39. The most significant increase will be in production of livestock and livestock products, which will reach an index of 265. How will the country meet the need?
Assuming that the increase in the acreage of cultivated land will be offset by the transfer of land from agricultural use to industrial and housing uses, the area will not rise in proportion with the increase in the demand for foodstuffs. The Gordon report forecasts that, by 1980, the cultivated area will be 176 million acres compared with 174 million obtaining today. From this we must conclude that these needs will be met mainly by a more rational use of land and by the adoption of a progressive agricultural policy, worked out and carried out to encourage our farmers and enable them to draw the same benefits from our country's wealth as people in other callings.
Mr. Chairman, there are several ways of increasing soil productivity, and I do not wish to dwell upon the technical details of production and soil improvement. Usually, a well-balanced agricultural policy like the one we had during the 22 years of Liberal administration gives good results in that respect.
That does not mean that changes are not called for. Never did our legislation require amending more than it does today, and it is precisely because of that fact that the Liberal government, in 1955, appointed a commission to make an inquiry into the country's agricultural progress and prospects. The commission brought down its report in 1957, and its findings should be used as the basis for making the changes which are necessary. The Liberal party understood this, and that is why novel concepts for agriculture were outlined to Canadians during the last election campaign. As for the Conservative party, it made a few vague promises whose implementation seems conspicuous by its absence. Just because the government enacted their Price Stabilization Act, they think they have found the solution to all the problems of agriculture. Although this act does not usher in any improvement
Supply-Agriculture
on the Price Support Act adopted by the Liberals, it was nonetheless as necessary as that act.
This act-a frequent subject of controversy during the last session-is still being widely criticized. It does not answer the need which gave rise to it. All you have to do to realize this is to look through the preamble, which reads as follows:
In order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment, and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy, thus to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income;-
This preamble looks fine on paper; but, for all practical purposes, what does it mean for the farmer. For many, it is a disappointment.
I have already informed the house of the meaning of this act for producers of milk intended for the manufacture of milk powder. I said then that the farmers got 10 cents less per cwt. of milk. I repeat at this time that in the province of Quebec farmers have been getting 10 cents less per cwt. since that legislation has been enacted. Moreover, manufacturers have lost $200,000 on the stocks they had on hand when the minister decided to lower the price. The price of milk in most Quebec areas as well as in the maritimes and in northern Ontario where milk powder is manufactured ranges from $2.75 to $2.80 per hundredweight. I may say that in the province of Quebec milk sells for $2.79 per cwt., whereas last year it was selling for $2.90.

I wish to make some suggestions which I am convinced would improve the lot of farmers, especially those who are in the low income group, if only the government would consent to putting my proposals into practice. This program could be implemented in two stages, the first in the immediate future and the second as opportunities arise. In this way the implementation would be simply a matter of time.
The first suggestion I wish to make which could be implemented immediately concerns the necessity of increasing the income of farmers in the eastern provinces and in northern Ontario and Quebec. As we are aware, the farmers of those regions produce chiefly milk, potatoes, tobacco and other crops of lesser importance. I do not wish to be repetitious in referring to the level of income of farmers, so, I shall merely say that in 1950 out of the 623,000 Canadian farms, 387,000 were selling products worth $2,500 or less, the average being $984. I might add that 80 per cent of the farm products came from 236,000 farms and 20 per cent came from the remaining 387,000. Nobody can establish that some of the farmers of the areas I have mentioned are not included in those 387,000 farms.
It is an established fact that in the east we could appreciably increase the yield of the harvest by the rational use of chemical fertilizers. A number of experiments have been carried out by the experimental farms and by the universities. Here is what one of our great specialists said. Mr. S. Cha-gnon, assistant deputy minister of the Department of Agriculture, several months ago wrote the following comment:
Once again our farmers claim that the cost of fertilizers is too high. Yet the work carried out on the experimental farms has shown that every dollar's worth of chemical fertilizers applied to pastures brings in $3.00 to $5.00 worth in the form of milk production. Although we have invested on our farms non-productive capital at a lightning pace, we have neglected to invest productive capital such as chemical or commercial fertilizers. It is most important to turn to a more intensive use of chemical fertilizers.
Dr. Ernest Mercier, superintendent of the Lennoxville experimental farm, says for his part:

Every dollar invested in chemical fertilizers applied to pastures brings in $2.00 to $4.00 in the form of beef.
Chemical fertilizers are complementary to manure and are indispensable to the maintenance of mineral balance. Chemical fertilizers are the best capital investment that the farmer can make.
An experiment was made by the New York state experimental farm to compare the production cost of one ton of milk by herds receiving various feeds and the cost was seen to be as follows: $12.10 when the animals were on pasture; $17.05 when they were fed corn silage; $25.35 when they were fed locally produced grain, and $34 when they were fed grain imported from the west.
I hope I have given a sufficiently comprehensive account of the experiments which have been carried out to prove the necessity of using chemical fertilizers, and the Minister of Agriculture should study the possibility of increasing their use by all possible means. One method which was used with success in the province of Quebec at a time when the province had a minister of agriculture who was interested more in agriculture than in electoralism was to grant a subsidy on every ton of chemical fertilizers purchased, in order to improve pastures. Another method would be to grant a certain quantity of fertilizer to the farmers for every milk cow they had on their farms. The money which the implementation of such a program would cost would be negligible because the program would increase production and, indirectly, lower the production cost of milk.
We of the province of Quebec and of the entire eastern part of the country consider these requirements to be justified to compensate for the loss caused to milk producers by the Minister of Agriculture when he brought down the support price of powdered skim milk by 2 cents a pound.
Another suggestion I wish to make to the Minister of Agriculture is that a special board be entrusted with the administration and implementation of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. I will not claim credit for this proposal, for it is set forth clearly in the report of the Gordon commission in the following terms:
This is an undertaking of such importance and delicacy that, in our opinion, it should be entrusted to a board of full-time members who would be relieved of other duties so that they could concentrate on anticipating the occurrence of emergency conditions and on determining the effects of particular prices on production and incomes.
In addition to recommending the level at which the prices of particular farm commodities might be supported from time to time, such a board might be left free to recommend also how this should be done. In general, two methods are available: the government can either purchase agricultural commodities when the prices fall below the stated support level, or it can allow farmers to dispose of their products at the prevailing market prices even though these may be below the support level.

and then make up the difference with deficiency payments. The latter procedure would avoid the difficulties in which the government would otherwise be involved in selling, storing, and disposing of surplus commodities. It would also have the advantage of letting the producer see the return that his products would bring him in a free market; and this knowledge might be expected to lead to a more realistic pattern of production. In our opinion, however, it is not possible to say that deficiency payments in all circumstances are to be preferred to direct price support; and an advisory judgment on this point, as well as on the level of support, might well be sought in each particular case from the board. Finally, we are convinced that neither the government nor the board in administering the price support program should be bound by any automatic formulae.
The prices stabilization board, which could be entrusted with finding new outlets for our products, would be able to perform much more valuable work than that done so far for the farmers by the adoption of the Agricultural Stabilization Act introduced in the house last January.
Since the Conservative government came to power, Mr. Chairman, the conditions of agriculture in general have been maintained due mainly to the commendable acts passed during the Liberal regime. In his speech on July 9 the minister stated that the improvement which has occurred arises out of the program adopted by the government, namely the adoption of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. I have shown that this act has had some very paltry results; that it has even brought about a loss for the skim milk producer. As for agricultural products, the prices of which have been stabilized, the minister knows as well as I do about the discontent which exists among so many producers.
Therefore we are far from the realization of the promises which the Minister of Agriculture, anxious to obtain votes in the province of Quebec, dangled in front of the farmers in a statement to the annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Montreal, reported in Le Devoir of January 30, 1958. The minister stated:
I am at present studying the possibility of setting up a form of insurance which would protect the farmers against calamity, floods, hail or drought.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps some hon. members, including the minister, will be surprised to see a lawyer by profession rise at this time and speak on agriculture. Last night we had a very good example of what a lawyer can do. I will try to do the same as he did.
It has been said that lawyers should know everything. I do not agree with that statement, but I do say that like any other citizen in this country or anywhere else, a lawyer 57071-3-186

has to try to learn something about almost everything, and this is what I tried to do about agriculture.
Sir, I would like to take this opportunity on the first item of the Department of Agriculture estimates to make a few remarks about agricultural problems and also to offer some suggestions which, if studied and implemented, would in my opinion be of some assistance to some of the farmers of our country.
(Translation):
During the few remarks I made in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, Mr. Chairman, I had the opportunity of speaking about employment, unemployment insurance and also on certain angles of education. However, I did not, at that time, mention any matter connected with farming. I therefore think I am justified to do so now.
As the minister knows, no doubt, I represent a semi-urban and semi-rural riding. As a matter of fact, there are three towns in my riding; all the rest consist in rural municipalities where a number of farmers try somehow to subsist and make both ends meet.
As everybody knows, our farmers in the province of Quebec, like in every other province of this country, work 16 to 18 hours a day when weather permits, and more especially in spring, summer and fall.
We might wonder whether our farmers in any area get a fair and equitable return for their labour. We should not forget that, in Canada, farming is mainly a family concern. The farm is a fundamental economic unit; and it is a sound one. But we should also keep in mind that farming is, to a certain extent, about to lose its character of a family concern in order to become a real industry.
I think that the government, in whom the voters showed their confidence on March 31 last, should concentrate on this problem and realize that the farms of our country might cease to be an economic family unit in order actually to become an agricultural industry.
It is up to this government, which has now assumed the responsibility of this country's business, to consider the situation and do whatever is required to protect our family industry and also to see to it that this farm industry develops at the same pace as other industries in this country.
The Liberal party had, in this matter, advocated a program which would have the

Supply-Agriculture
advantage of preserving the family character of farming, while providing for its expansion as an industry. Thus, during the last election campaign, we had undertaken to administer a new and bold program with a view to bettering the lot of our farm population in co-operation with the provinces.

With this aim in mind, we said that farmers, and particularly young farmers, should obtain the credit they need, i.e. long term credit to help finance the purchase of a farm and to make permanent improvements, as well as medium term credit for the purchase of farm animals and farm machinery.
Such, Mr. Chairman, was part of the program set up by the Liberal party with regard to farming. I sincerely believe that this program-I mean the setting up of this farm development bank-would have, as I said, the advantage of protecting the family character of our agriculture and, at the same time, provide for its development as a farming industry.
There is, Mr. Chairman, a particular subject I would like to deal with this morning. It was already mentioned last night by my friend, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine), and some hon. members have heard about it during previous sessions: I mean the problem of maple products. You know, Mr. Chairman, and I do not doubt that the Minister of Agriculture is also aware of the fact, that the maple product industry is of great importance to farmers in the province of Quebec. I should add that is also a significant part of farming development for the rural population in my riding of Megantic.
The hon. member for Beauce said last night that his riding was the main producer of maple products in the province of Quebec and, therefore, in the whole country. I might add that, according to statistics supplied by the agricultural division of the bureau of statistics of the department of industry and trade of the province of Quebec, the riding of Megantic is the second largest producer of maple products.
In 1951, Megantic had 2,497 occupied farms, including 1,332 reported to turn out maple products. In 1951, the number of suspended buckets was 1,823,602 i.e. an average of 1,369 buckets on each farm. The total production of maple syrup was 194,082 gallons in 1951, while the production sold or to be sold reached 170,598 gallons.

As to the total value sold or to be sold in 1951, it amounted, in my riding only, to $544,747 and the total value of maple product also for my riding only, reached $728,484. I am speaking of the riding of Megantic in its provincial boundaries, because the hon. Minister of Agriculture certainly knows that my riding of Megantic also includes part of the riding of Wolfe and part of the riding of Frontenac on a provincial basis. In the constituency of Frontenac, the value of maple products in 1951 was $495,778 whereas, for the constituency of Wolfe, it was $130,508.
It is impossible to obtain accurate data for those parts of the constituency of Megantic, since those statistics are strictly provincial.
Last year the attention of the government was directed to the maple products situation in the province of Q'uebec as in Canada as a whole, that is including parts of Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. This was done by members for the province of Quebec, notably by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Landry) and by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Laflamme). I believe and suggest that the hon. members representing those constituencies should consider those problems and make constructive suggestions, instead of spending their time commending government action, without knowing whether that action can be of any help to our people.
The Liberal government had recognized the importance of maple products, the oldest industry in the province of Quebec, and indeed in the whole country. Besides, that was the opinion expressed by the hon. senator Cyrille Vaillancourt in 1955. The Liberal government of the time had introduced subsidies to allow the exchange of sap buckets, because those buckets were then considered unsanitary, and their continued use might have harmed our export markets.
Here is, Mr. Chairman, what the hon. member for Portneuf, Dr. Pierre Gauthier, had to say on May 2, 1955, as found on page 3343 of the official report of the House of Commons Debates of that day:
A provision of the Food and Drugs Act of Canada bans the presence of lead in any kind of food. Therefore, regulations have been adopted to do away with soldered tins as containers of all kinds of canned food: pressed tin containers are now being used. For the same reason, tea, chocolate and cigarettes are wrapped in waxed or aluminum foil; no more lead paper Is used to wrap them.
That legislation had been enacted by the Liberal administration of the time. And,

while the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm may not know it, that provision was always opposed by Conservative members at the time. May I just remind you that Mr. Frank E. Lennard, a Progressive Conservative member, fought the measure so strongly on June 14, 1950, that a rather acrimonious debate ensued, because at that time he objected to those grants being made particularly to the province of Quebec, where there are more maple products growers than anywhere else in Canada.
It is a well known fact, Mr. Chairman, that the maple product industry, in the province of Quebec, is now in a slump.
The production of maple sugar has greatly decreased from 1937 to 1957. In fact, it has dropped from 4,020,000 pounds in 1937 to
536,000	pounds in 1957.
It will probably be said that this is a consequence of the indifference of the government of the time, but I want to emphasize that those matters relating to agriculture, especially in the province of Quebec, come under provincial jurisdiction, and that all the assistance the government of the time could give maple products growers was given them, as I have just said, when any farmer who wished to do so could replace his sap buckets.
Last night, I heard one hon. member say that the present government should keep up that policy of exchange of sap buckets. However, hon. members from the same party opposed this policy, and it was probably due to their action that the program was abandoned in 1955. There were, at the time, a considerable number of farmers who had benefited from this legislation and made the necessary changes.
With regard to maple syrup, the situation is just the opposite, and understandably so. The consumer who wants maple products prefers to buy syrup rather than sugar. As a matter of fact, in 1937, maple syrup production was only 780,000 gallons; in 1957, it reached a volume of 2,705,000 gallons. The gross value of that production for the year
1956-for we have as yet no statistics for 1957, amounted to $8,566,000 for all maple products, both syrup and sugar.
Mr. Chairman, this situation creates a problem which the government has to face, and I think it should more particularly study the issue raised with regard to maple products in the province of Quebec, in the eastern 57071-3-186J
Supply-Agriculture
part of Ontario, in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
The yield of maple products represents, for those who deal in them, an annual revenue varying from $1,000 to $2,000 and I can assure you that this revenue is welcome when the producer is able to get it. However, the situation offers a particular angle; quite a few farmers do not want to tap-and I know some in my riding who, last spring, right in the middle of the election campaign, refused to tap their maple trees because they did not know what conditions would obtain on the market and they also were in the dark about production costs and sales prices. This is probably no fault of the farmer himself, nor of the government. I do claim, however, that the government must study the matter and bring at least temporary solutions to these difficulties in order to assist those farmers, both in the province of Quebec and in the other three provinces who are engaged in the maple products industry.
My colleague from Beauce offered a few suggestions yesterday evening which are in all respects similar to those I had intended putting forward myself.
In fact, I have realized that the best way to facilitate the marketing of maple products was to carry on a proper sales promotion campaign on a national scale, not one limited solely to the province of Quebec. The campaign might also extend beyond our own borders.
It is an admitted fact that there is nothing more delicious than desserts prepared with maple syrup or maple sugar. That is why I think that every Canadian citizen should be able to buy those maple products at their local grocery or supermarket. No better way can they find of satisfying their palate. In doing so the consumer would help to a considerable extent those farmers who, each spring, are engaged in this particular phase of agricultural operations.
Mr. Chairman, the central government should take particular interest in a sales promotion campaign of this type. This matter could be considered at meetings between provincial and federal agricultural ministers. In this way an integrated sales promotion effort could be launched in all provinces to the advantage of farmers engaged in the production of maple syrup or maple sugar.
There is another way of helping the maple producer and that is through price support.

Supply-Agriculture
This might not perhaps be fully efficient, in view of the ups and downs of the market, but it would be a good thing, in my opinion, and not later than this year, to establish a support price for maple products. This would allow farmers engaged in maple product industry to make both ends meet and earn enough to meet their production costs. If the support price I am suggesting were inefficient-as I fear it would-it could be replaced by an adjustment grant or a deficiency payment.
In my opinion, it would be proper to extend throughout the whole country the price adjustment legislation enjoyed by prairie farmers.
As I see it, it is not just the western farmers who should derive benefit, as at present, from the Prairie Farm Assistance Act; all our farmers should enjoy these adjustment grants. This would not only mean that the maple producer would be just as sure of obtaining deficiency payments for his maple, but also that during unproductive years he would have the incentive to work on his maple trees-and also to hire helpers (for it is only fair to bear in mind that often, in such years, he works around the clock). In this way he could increase his annual income, and could more easily make ends meet.
It is my conviction, Mr. Chairman, that these suggestions are sound, and that the present government has the duty not only of giving them serious consideration, but of working out an appropriate formula for giving assistance to the farmers and producers of maple products in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, after listening to the dark outline of the fate of the farmer which the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) gave us last night, I considered it my duty to make some remarks and to bring to the attention of the house a report which appeared in Le Droit of June 23, 1958, under the heading:
Farmer fares better this year. He is recovering from last year's drop in income.

In 1957, farm income in Canada decreased by $403,300,000 to $1,053,900,000, the lowest figure in three years, as compared with $1,457,200,000 in 1956, the dominion bureau of statistics reported today.
For the first quarter of 1958, figures are more encouraging and it is estimated that, for that period, farm income will reach $604 million, an increase of $29 million over the corresponding period of 1957.
Those are the facts, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member took great pains in an endeavour

to show that agricultural prices stabilization was a failure. I wonder why, last year, the Liberal party supported the Conservative party by voting in favour of that legislation.
I would like to give some advice to the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska. Instead of spending his time talking against the beautiful province of Quebec, he should prepare his speeches more carefully, look for the facts and show them in their true perspective.
Those are, Mr. Chairman, the few remarks I wished to make following the gloomy speech of the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska.

That is a general summary of the criticisms we have heard during this debate, but I would just like to mention a few specific points.
The hon. member for Russell made, I think, quite a good speech, and he mentioned the way in which he himself had engaged in or had encouraged the production of flax.
I know he did a very useful piece of work from that point of view. But as to the hon. member for Timiskaming, I do not really think I should say very much about his comments. His knowledge of agriculture is indicated by this statement to be found at page 2173 of Hansard:
Mixed farming takes more from the soil than does the type of farming that is done in the west.

No statement could be more inaccurate than that, and it very well typifies and is an example of all the statements he made in his speech with regard to agriculture.
The hon. member for Gloucester went into the potato situation in Prince Edward Island in some detail. What he did really was to read into the record press statements from the Charlottetown Guardian of July 19, which I have here, and statements by Mr. Cullen, minister of agriculture for Prince Edward Island in which he was naturally trying to defend what he or the government of Prince Edward Island had or had not done in connection with the potato situation there.
I have here a compilation which is really a chronological case history of the potato situation in Prince Edward Island. In view of the fact that the hon. member for Gloucester put on the record this long statement by the minister of agriculture for Prince Edward Island, which is not correct, I think I had better correct it and the general false impression which may have been created by the statements made by the hon. member for Gloucester.
The first time this matter of potato support for Prince Edward Island came up was on May 20 of 1958-that is May 20 of this year-not on June 3, as was stated by Mr. Cullen. A letter was given to Mr. Pearsall, the chairman of the agricultural stabilization board, dated May 16-it arrived on May 20- requesting consideration of a guaranteed price for potato stocks remaining on hand as at July 1 or July 10 or July 15 at a price of $1.25 per hundredweight bulk for graded stock at loading point, or at the farm, if disposal for livestock feed from the farm was more convenient. A general discussion followed that proposal with representatives from Prince Edward Island, and no specific request was made by them for immediate action.
Then on June 3 and 4 Messrs. Cullen, Mac-Lennan and Burge, with one other representative, met the stabilization board. At that time the board proposed, following a study of the previous letter, a feed diversion program; that is, to divert these surplus potatoes into livestock feed. This proposal was rejected by the representatives as unworkable and on June 4 an offer of financial assistance, equivalent to what was being paid to New Brunswick on their starch diversion potatoes, was made although the specific amount was not stated.
On June 12 Mr. Pearsall called the island representatives on the long distance telephone, since they had claimed they were waiting for a further offer from the stabilization board. In this telephone call the board offered specifically 45 cents per bag with the
Supply-Agriculture
specific understanding that it was up to the Prince Edward Island potato growers either to accept or to reject this offer. On June 25 a wire was received-I may say this was 13 days later again-from Messrs. MacLennan and Burge accepting the offer on behalf of the potato marketing board but requesting that the total appropriation available be increased.
On June 26 there was a wire from Mr. Wright, the deputy minister of agriculture for Prince Edward Island, to Mr. Pearsall requesting details of the price support program. This wire was acknowledged the next day, on June 27, enclosing application forms.
On July 3 there was a wire from the minister of agriculture, Mr. Cullen, to myself raising the question of the quality of the potatoes and requesting relaxation of grade standards. Right up to this time they had not done anything about any of these things. This had been going on since May 26. Now they are making the claim that there was no delay on their part. If there was not delay there, where was it? It certainly was not here.
We received this wire on July 3 which raised the question of the quality of potatoes and requesting relaxation of grade standards. That wire was replied to in the negative at that time, on July 4. Then on July 11- in the meantime I may say there were a great many more representations-Mr. Eard-ley of the department's fruit and vegetable division, was sent down to Prince Edward Island to make an investigation on the spot and report back. He reported back to the board that indications were that about 300 cars of potatoes had not been marketed and that, based on a sample check, less than 10 per cent of these potatoes would qualify for Canada No. 1 grade.
After further discussion, on July 18 we advised these people that we would accept 75 per cent of the potatoes they still had on hand as having been eligible as first grade after inspection as to size and so forth, on the date on which this procedure should have been put into effect, say at the end of June. This was actually an extremely generous way of dealing with this relatively small amount of surplus potatoes in Prince Edward Island.

This is Liberal propaganda which comes from the office of the Leader of the Opposition, undoubtedly, and is intended to try to create the impression that the Liberals treated the potato growers of Prince Edward Island extremely well and so forth.
Actually as to the amount of money which was paid out for support may I say this, and I think I had better make this clear.
These amounts outlined by the hon. member for Gloucester and in the letters of hon. members of another place were not the amounts which were paid out for Prince Edward Island potatoes. Very little was paid out for Prince Edward Island potatoes in most of these years, and in many years nothing was paid. That was the amount paid out to support potato growers across the country as a whole, and I may indicate that under the agricultural prices support act, as it was, and the stabilization act as it is now, in only

one year, 1948-49, was more money paid out for potatoes than in the year we completed a year ago this spring-no, less than a year ago-that is, for the crop of 1956-57. What the figures will be for the year 1957-58 we do not know yet, because a great many of the claims have not yet come in. So much for the potato situation in Prince Edward Island.
The hon. member for Beauce brought up the matter of maple sap buckets. I should like to point out to him that the party to which he belonged when they were in power were the people who did away with this subsidy. Why come complaining to us because the subsidy has been removed? It was done away with by his own party.
The hon. member for Kootenay West dealt particularly with farm credit, and paid a very well deserved tribute to the work the Veterans' Land Act people have done in connection with this. I fully agree with the remarks he made in connection with how well the credit facilities extended under the Veterans' Land Act have been supervised, how high a degree of repayment there has been, and how satisfactory that scheme has been, and as I have said on many occasions previously I hope and expect that we will be able to incorporate something along these lines in the improved farm credit scheme and legislation which we expect to bring forward.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont needs to look up his history. He made the statement that our great research facilities had been instituted by the Liberal government. If he will look into the matter he will find that these research facilities were started long before the past Liberal government came into existence. In fact they were started shortly after confederation in the way of some experimental farms and things of that kind, so he does not need to think the former government can take credit for the research facilities we have in agriculture, because these have been built up under many administrations over a long period.
And his criticisms, again, of the organization of the research facilities and the experimental farm service is a criticism of his own previous government. I may say that we are taking steps at the present time to reorganize the Department of Agriculture, and I will have a statement to make in that connection before this debate is over.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska complained about the support price of skimmed milk powder having been reduced from 17 cents to 15 cents, as though this were a terrible thing. I wonder if he has heard about the fact that before the price of milk

powder was reduced from 17 cents to 15 cents, the price of butter was increased from 58 cents to 64 cents, an increase of 6 cents a pound.
The less he or any other Liberal member says about the price of skimmed milk powder the better off they will be, because they, and the previous Liberal government, created an absolutely impossible situation as far as skimmed milk powder was concerned. They put in a support price of 17 cents, which was about 5 or 6 cents higher than the world market price, and took no steps whatever to prevent skimmed milk powder coming in from any country in the world where there was a surplus.
The inevitable result was that when I became Minister of Agriculture I found a terrible accumulation of dried skimmed milk powder which had been coming in from the United States, New Zealand, Holland, and even Great Britain, which is a deficiency area with regard to dairy products. It was an example of terribly bad administration and policy on the part of the previous Liberal government. We, of course, had to put in import control in order to stop that flood of powder coming into this country and completely disrupting our market.
Those, I think, are the only points about which I need say anything now.

Mr. Chairman, when I was interrupted in the course of my remarks on the agricultural program which I was suggesting to the government, I was about to explain a policy which should be adopted by the government and whose results would be far-reaching.
First of all, there is the inquiry into soil utilization and conservation, launched in 1955 under the Liberal government.
As compared with seven meetings held during 1957, there have only been three or four since the Conservative party came to power. I feel the present government should instil some vigour into this work so as to introduce a program which would go hand in hand with the soil study that will have been accomplished, especially in eastern Canada. Everyone versed in agriculture says it is necessary to classify our soil so as to put it to the best use in the various areas and to formulate the most fitting conservation recommendations.
Agricultural experts have noted that 46 per cent of the soil at Lake St. John has been seriously affected by erosion (350,000 acres out of the total of 860,000 acres of reclaimed soil). I deplore that the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) is not present in the house to benefit from this information in the interests of the farmers of this area.
The same phenomena can be observed in the Joliette area. Producers of flue-cured tobacco there are only too well aware of the destructiveness of wind in these sandy regions.
Indeed, the same phenomena arise everywhere in Canada-perhaps on a bigger scale in flat country.

One can get a good idea of the damage done by erosion in looking at our rivers after a heavy rain. The water becomes dirty and muddy and carries away the best elements of the soil. Such damage caused by the constant erosion of our lands may bring upon us the calamity of which a poet has said: "Old empires have been destroyed as much by the loss of their soil as by the sword of their enemies."
Mr. Auguste Scott, a distinguished professor at the Agricultural College of Ste-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere, had this to say about the steps to be taken to control soil erosion:
We should first of all undertake a thorough study of our soil and its fertility. At the same time, an education campaign should be organized among the farmers, additional meteorological stations should be created and research centres established.
More specifically, Professor Scott advocates the improvement of the fertility of poor soils or of soils which have lost their fertility through erosion. Among the most efficient means of warding off that danger, he suggests crop rotation and the use of lime and of chemical and organic fertilizers. He also recommended the establishment of a soil conservation board. I would like the Minister of Agriculture to take note of my observations concerning this soil conservation board.
The work of such an organization should be carried out as soon as possible so that its recommendations may be implemented without delay.
The second step would consist in improving the Farm Loan Act to increase the assessment value of the property given in guarantee, in raising the maximum amount and in establishing a supervision service made up of competent agricultural experts who would direct and advise the borrowers.
As I have had the opportunity of making a few brief comments on that matter, I will not add anything more for the time being.
A third step, which would certainly bring results although over a longer period, would be the expansion of our farm research services.
I am happy to pay tribute to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) who dealt thoroughly with that question and with whom I agree wholeheartedly.
The United States announced a few months ago that they were increasing their agricultural research budget by $50 million. At that time, many Americans criticized that measure, stating that the amount was inadequate and was lagging 20 years behind.

We could easily say the same thing about Canada. We are lagging behind 20 years, since most of the discoveries that we are applying to our agricultural and processing methods come from the United States.
This research should not have as its sole aim to increase the yield by acre or by livestock unit; it should also seek means of applying our products to other industrial uses.
All who are interested in agriculture recognize that, if we adopted all the new methods to increase the yield per acre, the development of new varieties of cereals, new fertilizers and chemical products to fight those plagues brought about by insects and plant diseases, our farmers would double the yield of their farm. Is not such a possibility of increasing the yields of our farms a sufficient reason to vote more money for research work?
The director of the federal research laboratory in the prairie provinces, in Saskatoon, Mr. Ledingham, made an interesting statement last November. I quote:
(Text):
He suggested, among other things, that land capable of producing high quality bread wheat was now being used for oil seed crop production while land in northern sections of the prairies, where oil seed crops could be grown effectively, is being used to produce low quality wheat. He mentioned recent developments in the laboratory in finding industrial uses for agricultural products, one of them the production of a fibreboard from wheat straw.
In Canada the cost of agricultural research, when measured against its contribution to the national welfare, has never been high. But there is a need for intensification of such research. There seems to be a valid argument for spending increased funds on research that may provide permanent solutions to the problem of agricultural surpluses rather than invest ever-increasing amounts on support of plans that in the United States particularly have only worsened this particular farm problem. I doubt if I have any questions to ask the minister, but I would like

to make one or two observations on this matter. The act, as we know, is there to protect us as well as the farmers, and with respect to cattle-and here I am referring to tuberculosis-there is some background information I would like to give the house in order to make myself clear. I have in mind a recent incident in Bruce riding.
A large dairy herd in a restricted area had been accredited for quite a number of years and had a clear bill at each inspection. Recently it was found, however, that there were 12 reactors in the herd, which was quite a surprise to the owner and no doubt also to the veterinary surgeon who discovered this condition. I understand there was some discussion with the veterinary people who did the testing and also the inspector for the district but nothing could be done, apparently, or was not done. These 12 valuable cows went to Toronto and had to be killed, although there was no visible sign of tuberculosis in any of the 12 animals.
In Toronto they went through the ordinary channels in the packing houses and the owner of the herd is still not convinced that a mistake was not made. He does not know, of course, but he is not convinced that the veterinary surgeon was correct, and in speaking to the officials of the health of animals branch I was informed that there are certain cases where an animal is infected, yet it does not show after it has been killed, but that if a more thorough examination of the carcass was made the probabilities are that such a disease would show up. In fact I am assured it would though it would take a lot of research work on the carcass to be sure
The suggestion I would like to throw out to the minister is that in the first instance these 12 animals should have been quarantined and re-tested later on and that in the second place if they had to go to Toronto as a group of 12 and did not show any sign of infection, I think there should be a regulation that the inspectors should have tried to go further and confirm that the animals had really been infected. In these circumstances this owner has suffered a considerable loss, and everything should be done to find out whether or not a mistake has occurred. I am not saying the veterinary surgeon made a mistake at all, but it does look as though there was some doubt. If such was found out, namely that such cattle were taken out and slaughtered, I think in all fairness the owner of the cattle should be recompensed for his loss, at least in part.

I have had a few complaints along this line with regard to cattle which were tuberculin tested and showed as reactors and then, when they went in for

slaughter, there was found on post-mortem examination no definite sign of tuberculosis, but I understand from the experts in this line that this happens fairly frequently. If the tuberculosis is in the early stages the test which is made is very reliable in indicating that tuberculosis is present in the animal, but post-mortem examination quite frequently will not show that any definite deterioration has taken place. The test picks out the t.b. infected cattle before what are known as gross lesions develop which would be detected on post-mortem.
The fact that no gross lesions were found in these particular cattle does not mean that they did not have tuberculosis. One of the great values of the test is that it picks out animals before the disease has developed sufficiently so that the risk of infection to other cattle is very greatly increased. I think also we must be fairly stringent if we are to have a tuberculosis testing program such as we have, and which has resulted in tuberculosis in cattle having been reduced from something like about 4 per cent in 1923 to less than one-tenth of one per cent at present of cattle tested that are reactors. In order to be able to export our cattle, particularly dairy cattle, freely to the United States and other countries we must have a tuberculosis testing program of this kind in effect. It is hard on a particular farmer who has a large part of his herd go down. Nevertheless, in the interests of farmers generally in this country and in the interests of the general economy I think we must be fairly stringent as far as these tuberculosis testing programs are concerned.

I have sat quietly here without interrupting the minister, and yet when I attempt to utter a single sentence he interrupts me.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister tell us under what terms and conditions eggs are destroyed, and in what quantity?

Mr. Chairman, this is an old classification which has been in the estimates for some years. It is due to the fact that Newcastle's disease and fowl typhoid can

Supply-Agriculture
both be transmitted through the egg. Therefore provision was made for the destruction of eggs at a time when these diseases were prevalent. There was an outbreak of Newcastle disease about three or four years ago, and some discussion occurred at that time.

Item agreed to.
Livestock and poultry-
21.	Livestock and poultry production, including premiums on pure-bred sires and contributions for livestock improvement, $1,938,438.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a word about the production of lambs and wool in Canada. I saw a recent estimate which indicated that Canada imports 15 million pounds of lamb a year. Canada raises 1,500,000 sheep, but this production could be raised to 10 million. Could the minister tell us what he intends to do to improve the production of sheep in Canada?

Mr. Chairman, we have already taken very definite steps in order to increase sheep production in Canada. We put into effect under the Agricultural Stabilization Act a support price of 60 cents a pound for wool. A two-day conference of sheep producers from all over Canada was convened in Ottawa, and this action was taken in response to their request concerning what effective steps might be taken in order to improve and increase the production of sheep in Canada. They were unanimous in saying that a support price for wool was the most important thing to be done, and as a result we put into effect this support price for wool.
I might say that of all the measures we have taken to improve agricultural prices in Canada, and all the steps we have taken under the Agricultural Stabilization Act and otherwise, this particular step of putting this support price under wool has resulted in more letters of thanks than any other single thing we have done. Sheep men from all over Canada have written thanking me most sincerely for having taken this step as far as the sheep industry is concerned.

This policy was indeed necessary and I too thank the minister, but it is not what we want to increase the production of lambs. We have a considerable area of marginal land in Canada in crops which could be put to better use as pastures. These pastures could be improved at little

cost. They should be classified for this purpose following an investigation of land use. That is why I wish to ask the minister whether the land use investigation is being pursued by the special committee of the other place?

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the hon. member that we could have and should have a great deal more sheep production in Canada. That is why I called this meeting of those sheep people in order to get their advice as to what steps to take. As I say they, unlike the hon. member, were unanimous in saying that the most important thing was to put this support price under wool. In addition they recommended various other steps of a less important nature. In order to carry on this work we have asked for a special grant in order to set up a sheep committee, or an advisory group, so there can be a continuing body during the next year to carry on the investigation of the sheep industry and to make recommendations as to the best steps to take to improve and enlarge that industry.

Item agreed to.
22.	Supervision of race track betting, $279,988.

This is an appropriation having to do with racetrack betting. As I understand it, this item is under the control of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I wonder why this item is not in the Department of Justice estimates, because the R.C.M.P. come under the Department of Justice. There is an increase of $20,000 in this vote, and I would like to know why?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is quite incorrect. If he will refer to the Criminal Code he will see that it assigns the supervision of racetrack betting to the Minister of Agriculture, and it is carried out under the supervision of this department. It is quite true that the mounted police are employed as far as some of the supervisory work is concerned, but they are employed under the supervision of or by this department. Whilst they are engaged on those racetrack activities the Department of Agriculture pays their expenses.
They are under the control of the Department of Justice?

They are not under the control of the Department of Justice when they are working on this racetrack activity; they are under the control of the Department of Agriculture. As I said, we pay their expenses. Normally, of course, the mounted

police are under the control of the Department of Justice. We have them, you might say, on loan for some of the work of supervising racetracks.

Can the minister tell us whether any of these funds are recoverable from the revenue from racetracks? I understand the provinces get quite a bit of revenue from the racetracks. Why should they not supervise the tracks?

Mr. Chairman, we receive one-half of one per cent of the moneys wagered, and that has produced a revenue very greatly in excess of what we have been spending in recent years. In other words, the department was making money by supervising betting at the racetracks. I might say that the people engaged in racing horses and in carrying on racing were, I think, justifiably put out that we were making a great deal more than we were spending in the supervision of racing, and they have been requesting for many years that the department undertake what they call an "eye in the sky" camera which follows the horses around the track, as a result of which they have a record of any irregularities. It is a means of making sure that the running of the race is carried on according to the rules, which also involves salivary and urinary tests. A few months ago I agreed to assume the cost of carrying on these operations, and we expect as a result that the revenues and the expenditures will be much more nearly balanced in the future.

I am informed it was in 1955.

Has the minister given any
consideration to raising the $100,000 ceiling? It seems to me, with the cost of buildings today and the very useful purpose to which they can be put, such a ceiling perhaps should be increased. Well, Mr. Chairman, this
particular figure is the estimate of the officials of the department as to what the grants which have been applied for and which cover work which will be completed during the year will amount to. It so happens that in this particular year the estimate is, as the hon. member says, $5,000 less than it was in the previous year.

themselves over the plans and as a result they did not get started on their building. They now inform us that this year their building will require this amount so that is the amount we have put in the estimates.
