Item agreed to.
29.	Subsidies for cold storage warehouses under the Cold Storage Act, in the amounts detailed in the estimates $445,916.
First of all I should like to ask the minister what is the reason for cutting in half the amount of money to be expended under the Cold Storage Act.

We decided, as the result of a considerable number of representations that had been made to us, that the amount of cold storage now existing made it unnecessary for us to subsidize everybody who wanted to go into the cold storage business. In the past we paid out quite large subsidies to large commercial concerns which were building big cold storage warehouses across the country. As a result of a review of the matter a few months ago I had the regulations changed so that the amount of grant would be limited to $50,000 in the case of

any one cold storage project. The purpose was to ensure that this form of assistance was extended as far as possible to farmers' and fishermen's co-operatives and organizations of that sort which in many cases still need to build comparatively small cold storage warehouses and require assistance whereas we did not think it was necessary to continue that type of assistance to large commercial concerns. As a result, the amount of money that will be expended will be very much reduced and that is why the item is reduced.
I understand that formerly there was no limit to the total subsidy but there was a limit in terms of a percentage of the total cost, a maximum of one-third of the cost or something of that sort.

That is correct. There was no limit on the total cost of the cold storage building which was erected. We paid one-third of the cost and, of course, we still pay one-third of the cost. There is no change in that regard but this upper limit of $50,000 has been imposed which means that in the future anybody who builds a $3 million cold storage plant will not get a $1 million subsidy.

It may seem strange-I found it strange when it came to my attention- that fishermen's problems should be dealt with in the department of agriculture but, as the minister has said, subsidy payments under the Cold Storage Act are also payable to fishermen's co-operatives to enable them to build fish cold storage plants.
Undoubtedly the matter to which I wish to refer has been drawn to the attention of the minister or his officials. I wish to make a formal plea on behalf of the Prince Rupert fishermen's co-operative association. When there was no limit to the subsidy other than one-third of the total cost the Prince Rupert fishermen's co-operative made plans to build a cold storage plant having in mind that they would receive a subsidy of one-third of the total cost from the department. I believe they received approval to go ahead some few years ago but difficulties then arose between the Prince Rupert fishermen's co-operative and another co-operative in Vancouver and they decided to delay the building of the cold storage plant.
However, they have now made plans to proceed with it without realizing that a $50,000 ceiling has been placed on the subsidy they will be able to receive under the Cold Storage Act. If the minister feels it is necessary to place a limit of $50,000 on the subsidy because of the huge cold storage plants being built costing millions of dollars, I ask him very seriously, speaking particularly

of the Prince Rupert fishermen's co-operative although there may be other co-operatives or companies in the same boat, whether he would not consider relaxing the regulation in the case of the Prince Rupert fishermen's co-operative and any other groups in the position of having developed their plans on the assumption they would receive a subsidy amounting to one-third of the total cost. Otherwise, now that they are ready to proceed they will be hampered by the fact that a limit has been placed on the subsidy they had expected to receive.
I think if the minister would undertake to do that he would certainly find, so far as the Rupert fishermen's co-op is concerned, he would assist them immeasurably in the expansion of their cold storage locker and that if there are other cases which fall into the same category I am sure this sort of action would be greatly appreciated. I hope the minister will undertake to take some steps in the direction of relaxing the $50,000 limit which applies to those who have unfortunately found themselves having to raise a few thousand more dollars than they had originally thought would be necessary.

One thing I mentioned
before and which I should like to make sure the members of the committee understand is that these subsidies are available only to people to erect public cold storages, whether it be a co-op or an individual enterprise. It must not only be a public cold storage but it must remain so, otherwise the subsidy is repayable. I do not know whether this particular co-op wants the cold storage entirely for its own operations or not but in any event to do what the hon. member asks would really mean we would have to go back about four years. These people, I am informed, had an agreement to build a cold storage but at the end of the year they had still not raised the money or completed their plans, and they asked for an extension. They got three such extensions and eventually the agreement became void.
If we were to go back and revise agreements entered into during the past five years I think the hon. member will recognize we would be in a practically impossible situation. I might also tell him that it would mean an expenditure of several million more dollars in subsidies for a considerable number of private enterprises which had agreements but which did not raise the money or complete their plans so that their agreements lapsed. If we were to do as the hon. member asks and recognize this voided agreement which is now five years old, we would have to do the same thing for everybody and there are a large number of such old agreements. This would
Supply-Agriculture
create an extremely awkward situation and problem and would also, I think, be unfair to those people who have been in the cold storage business for years and to the many smaller farmers' and fishermen's co-operatives which have built cold storages.

I would like to carry on to amplify this thought. I was not suggesting we should go back four or five years and renew every old agreement. I am only stating the circumstances in so far as the Rupert fishermen's co-op is concerned.
That was the situation with the Rupert co-op.

Yes, I quite appreciate that but I am also saying it has not been because of lack of desire or need that that co-op did not proceed with their expansion program but I think it is equally unfair to the Rupert co-op or to any other co-op or group wanting to operate and own its plant to allow them to develop their plans on the assumption that they would receive a one-third grant and then, when they are ready to definitely proceed, to find out that the subsidy is not there and that they are going to have to raise the difference between the one-third and the $50,000 if the cost is more than $150,000, as it is in this case. I think it is equally unfair to place co-op associations and others in a position of assuming that they are going to get it in the first place and then suddenly to discover they must raise additional capital and that their plan for orderly marketing and protection of foodstuffs-in this case fish-are all upset. I know the minister is very able and I am sure that if he tries hard enough he will find some way around this difficulty.

Mr. Chairman, I do not see that there is anything unfair in this situation. This particular organization had four years to build its warehouse; they had an agreement which lapsed and it was extended three successive times. The agreement was for one year and it eventually lapsed altogether and is now void. I do not think there is anything unfair there at all. They had four years in which to mature their plans and they did not do so. It is much the same thing as if I entered a contract to buy a car for so much money and I did not go ahead and buy the car but four years later I came along wanting to get a car of that year's model at the same price I had contracted for four years earlier. It is just not a reasonable proposition.

Could I ask this one question: did the minister say the regulation was changed two or three months ago?

Supply-Agriculture
No, I think it was six months ago.

At any rate it was a relatively short time ago. Did the minister or did any of his officials discover that groups or organizations or companies had in years past received subsidies under the Cold Storage Act and its one-third provision although they were not entitled to do so?

I am informed that nothing is known along that line, but I can tell my friend that every application for a subsidy is very carefully investigated and we do turn down a considerable number. Many people put in applications although they have not met the regulations; they start to build their cold storage and then they come along and ask for a subsidy. Under the act we cannot pay it to them and we get a great many complaints from people who think they should get a subsidy and do not get one. I can certainly assure the hon. member that these applications are very carefully investigated before a subsidy is paid and before an agreement is entered into to see that the projected cold storage will meet all the requirements of the regulations laid down and that the expenditures for building are very carefully checked so that we can be sure we are not paying more than the one-third share called for by the agreement.

Mr. Chairman, this may have a bearing on the matter. I wonder if there are statistics available as to the average or general cost of fish cold storage as related to the general or average cost of cold storage for garden products, meats and so on?

We have not any cost figures here, Mr. Chairman, but my officials inform me that the lower the temperature required the higher the cost, and therefore the cold storage for fish as opposed to that for fruit and vegetables would entirely depend on the amount of space devoted to low temperatures. In the present cold storage for fruits and vegetables a considerable amount of space is for deep-freezing purposes, for fast-freezing of fruits and vegetables and to keep them in that frozen form for long periods of time. It may therefore be that at the present time the cost of fruit and vegetable cold storage is more expensive than that required for fish, but that again would depend on the proportion of space required for these low temperatures.

I should like to proceed a little bit further. As I said earlier, it seemed to be somewhat odd to me when I discovered these subsidies for fish cold storage warehouses would come under the Department of

Agriculture. I would have normally expected that subsidies for fish cold storage would more properly be administered by the Department of Fisheries, not that I am saying that the administration has not been good or otherwise. However, it would appear to me to be a more sensible division or application of it, inasmuch as the products which are stored and used are different, to divide the administration as it applies to fish cold storage plants and to place that under the Department of Fisheries where they deal every day with fish, fish products, fish marketing services, price supports, research and everything else. I wonder whether some consideration would not be given to that suggestion.

The reason we administer this matter is that there is only one Cold Storage Act and it is provided that it shall be administered by the Department of Agriculture. The number of cold storages built for fish products is very small in comparison with the number built for meat, fruit, vegetables, butter, cheese and all the other products and it is not sufficient to justify a separate administration for fish cold storages. The actual practice is that when we get an application in for a fish cold storage we promptly send it over to the Department of Fisheries and ask them to investigate it and give us a report on it before we proceed any further.
Did the minister say "properly" or promptly?
We promptly send it over to the Department of Fisheries. As I say we get their report before we proceed any further on it.

I should like to ask another question. I am sorry I did not do this earlier and I hope the minister will not mind my trying to get this information for my own sake. It is purely for that purpose at the moment. I understood the minister to say that the reason for the placing of a ceiling of $50,000 was that there had been some fairly heavy expenditures made under this act in the past to the huge cold storage groups and therefore it was felt to be unnecessary to be continually pumping federal government money into these cold storage operations. Is that generally what the reason was?

As I indicated previously, the thing is that I received a considerable number of representations from people who already had cold storages in existence to the effect that the subsidy which we were through the department making available was resulting in cold storage space being overbuilt in their particular areas and was having the effect or was going to have the effect

of forcing them out of business with their existing cold storage. We were putting up a third of the cost for the new cold storage.
After looking into the matter it seemed to me that in many cases this was a fairly valid complaint. Also on looking over the history of it and on getting the figures as to the amount of cold storage which we have in Canada and the percentage of occupancy, I was particularly struck by the fact that the percentage of occupancy in the cold storages in Canada was not very high. I have forgotten the exact figures but I think it did not run much more than 50 per cent. I am informed that my memory on that matter is correct and that it ran about 50 per cent. With occupancy of existing cold storages at only about 50 per cent and running up to 70 per cent in some seasons, it seemed to me to be an unjustifiable use of public money to subsidize the construction of further cold storages except those required in certain areas, as I say, by farmers and fishermen's co-operatives in order to hold their product until they could market it. For those reasons I decided to limit the amount of the grant to $50,000.

May I inquire whether those representations and the results of the study that was made and the realization that there was too much cold storage space and not enough use being made of it and so on apply to agricultural cold storage space or just that for fish? How did the fish cold storage plants fit into that study?

The figures that I have compiled cover all the cold storages across the country. What the break-down was between the ones which were used entirely or primarily for fish, I do not know. The hon. member probably knows that there are a number of cold storages which are used for both fish and agricultural products.

The minister has said that there is an upper limit of $50,000 put on assistance under this act. Would he explain why it is that at page 126 of the details of assistance, there are some grants which are well in excess of $50,000 for next year.

Those are to cover contracts which were already in existence before the limit of $50,000 was put on. In other words, there were a considerable number of contracts which had been entered into by the government of which the Leader of the Opposition was a member, and we have not finished paying out under those; the construction was still going on or if it was completed, a complete check of it had not been made and the settlement had not yet been made. All those in excess of that amount which you see in the details are old contracts

which were in existence when the change was made; and of course we did not make this change retroactive and disturb the old contracts.
Would that explanation also cover the items in the supplementary estimates for assistance under this act?

The deputy minister is still looking up those items but I am quite sure it would, yes; because since we made this change no cold storage subsidies have been authorized in excess of $50,000. If there are any in there in excess of $50,000, they must be old contracts.
Even in the supplementary estimates?
Yes.

I should like to substantiate the minister's advice in that respect. I happen to be in the cold storage business myself in Saskatchewan and as president of the Saskatchewan locker operators association I know there has been a definite trend in the last few years away from the placing of food in cold storage plants owing to the advent of home freezers. It is a definite trend. It is something that we must face up to. But I think the minister's advice in that respect is quite right.

I feel that the Minister of Agriculture is making a mistake in putting this arbitrary limit of $50,000 on any grant that may be made to a cold storage firm. If the minister is correct in saying that in certain areas there has been over-building and that the amount of space that is used is too low, surely that would be a factor in considering any individual application-*
It is.

-as to whether or not storage in a given area were in fact needed. But it would seem to me that the instance of Prince Rupert, shall we say, or in any other instance-I do not claim to be acquainted with this case that has been raised-it would be a greater service to the agricultural industry and to consumers generally to judge each case on its merits rather than to say that an arbitrary limit of $50,000 is going to be placed on the amount that can be paid for any cold sorage. As far as farmers' cooperatives, fishermen's co-operatives or other co-operatives may be concerned, I think the $50,000 limit is going to mean a hardship for some of them. Even in this very estimate that is under consideration there is a cooperative in the province of Quebec that is to get a grant of $105,884. If an arbitrary limit of $50,000 were set, then of course that

Supply-Agriculture
co-operative would get a good deal less. For the minister to say that this is for co-operatives, that we are going to give it to cooperatives through a kind of back door method by setting a $50,000 ceiling, is something that I do not think should be done. I do not think that is the way to administer anything.
If this is designed to help co-operatives, why does the minister not put in a clause saying that subsidies for co-operative organizations for the building of cold storage plants may be one-third of the cost without regard to a ceiling. I do not think it is possible to say we are putting on a $50,000 ceiling and at the same time say the whole program is for the purpose of assisting cooperatives. I can remember when I came into this chamber in 1946 or 1947, a couple of years after I was elected there was a long discussion on this very question. At that time, as I remember the discussion, the department was not following the practice of allowing co-operatives building locker plants to be eligible for this subsidy; it was a subsidy for large bulk storage plants. After a good deal of discussion, the minister of agriculture of that day, the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, agreed it should be extended to include co-operative lockers and I think I had the honour of having a subsidy paid to a locker plant in my constituency, one of the very first to take advantage of it.
We have heard it said in these discussions by members on all sides of the house that one of the reasons there is such a tremendous fluctuation in the price of perishable farm products is that ample storage is not available. I have listened to the Minister of Agriculture today, and I am not convinced that this ceiling is the way to administer cold storage facility development. If the government feels that in a given area no new storage facilities are required, let us have no subsidy at all. But if an organization, and particularly a co-operative association, can make a case for the building of a storage plant which costs in excess of $150,000, then I suggest it is not good business from the standpoint of the welfare of this nation to place an arbitrary ceiling on this item. I think the reduction from $915,000 in the former estimate to $445,000 in this year's estimate, together with a look at the estimates which show that there are a number receiving amounts in excess of $50,000, means that the government is going a long way toward wiping out a cold storage program which has been built up step by step, and which is serving a very useful purpose.

I am not arguing with the hon. member that there was not a need for

a cold storage program of this sort in the past, but I would once more draw to his attention the fact that the surveys I have carried out showed that the existing cold storage is only being used to 50 per cent of capacity. Under the circumstances, what excuse is there for using the taxpayers' money to subsidize in large amounts the building of more storage? There is no excuse for it at all. I would have done away with this altogether except that there still exists the need for more storage-small storage facilities-in isolated parts of the country, or in parts of the country which are more or less isolated. I said that most of the people who would benefit under the present regulations with a limit of $50,000 are farmers' and fishermen's co-operatives in areas which are to some extent isolated. But we do not want to limit this to co-operatives. Any group of farmers that wants to build a cold storage plant with public facilities, for instance, may receive a subsidy. These are the very people who need to be helped and I think from all the information I have been able to gather that $50,000 is quite adequate. If you put it at more than $50,000 you are in effect subsidizing the building of big cold storage plants which are just going to take storage business away from other large cold storage plants already in existence.

I wonder if the minister could tell me how many cold storage plants there are which deal exclusively or, in the main, with agricultural products; how many deal exclusively, or in the main with fish; and how many handle both agricultural products and fish in combination.
We have not those figures, but we could have them compiled by the department and I would be glad to do that and send them to the hon. member.
Do I understand that the figures are not yet compiled but that this could be done?
Yes.

The minister has informed the committee that he has conducted a survey and that he has discovered that the present storage facilities, or the operators of them, needed protection and that there did not appear to be any need for additional storage facilities.
No. I did not make either of those statements.
Perhaps the minister will let me finish.
Don't put words into my mouth that I did not utter.

I do not want to get into the same sort of altercation with the minister as I did yesterday, but a good way to begin one would be by making these interruptions. The minister said he had conducted a survey.
That is right.
And that as a result of that survey he had discovered certain things. Is that right?
That there was a 50 per cent occupancy.
Sometimes going up to 70 or 75 per cent, I forget which figure the minister used.
Seventy.

I attempted to discover from the minister what division there was with respect to fish cold storage and agricultural products cold storage, and he does not know the figures, though he says he can have them compiled and send them to me. But they will not do me any good. What the minister has just admitted is that in the course of the examination he conducted he did not attempt to discriminate between cold storage facilities for agricultural products and cold storage facilities for fisheries products. He just made a complete survey across the board, said this represented the general picture as far as cold storage is concerned, made no attempt to differentiate between the two products and decided that the ceiling of $50,000 would be appropriate.
I will go one step further and say that the reduction from $915,000 to $445,000, a sum equal to less than half of the former estimate, together with the $50,000 limit, is an indication that the main estimates will be cut in half again next year, because there will not be these large sums of money payable and I suggest to the minister with all due respect to what he may have said-and I have no intention of putting words into his mouth-that if he had made as thorough an investigation of this subject as he made of the question raised yesterday by the hon. member for Laurier, he would have discovered that an entirely different picture exists with respect to agricultural cold storage.
The hon. member is, in effect, accusing me of not knowing what I am doing and not having the information on which to do it.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I wish the minister would not put words in my mouth.

Mr. Chairman, I was not putting words in the hon. member's mouth. I said that in effect this was what he was 57071-3-187

saying. I ventured to suggest that in connection with cold storage the only information he has relates to the situation at Prince Rupert. I think he would be better advised to find out what the situation is with regard to cold storage across Canada before he begins making these broad, general sweeping statements.
The investigation which we carried on with respect to occupancy of cold storage facilities was very complete. I indicated some time before that a large number of these facilities are used for both fish and agricultural products. The hon. member is complaining because I do not have here a break-down as to the exact number which are used for fish only, the exact number used for both fish and agricultural products and the number used for other commodities. That would be an extensive compilation job. I have informed the hon. member that it could be done and I shall be glad to have it undertaken and send him the information but in the meantime I take objection to his making broad statements which are to the effect that we did not know what we were doing when we did this.

I could very easily agree with the minister on that point but I will not. With all due respect to him and his department I point out that when I opened my remarks I said I was referring specifically to the Price Rupert fishermen's co-operative association and that was it. I was not talking about fish cold storage plants throughout Canada or agricultural cold storage plants. Regardless of whether or not the minister knew what he was doing-and that is for him and not me to decide-he looked at the entire picture and decided that because certain conditions existed the subsidy would have application to everybody regardless of the merits of the individual case. I am objecting to the application of the subsidy not being based on the merits of individual cases without limitations being placed upon it.

I wonder if the minister could tell us if a survey was taken for only cine year or over a period of years. Could he also tell the committee whether the 50 per cent occupancy of cold storage is a standard figure for a number of years or whether it has been diminishing rapidly as time went on? I hasten to admit that I am no authority about cold storage facilities but it would seem to me that if cold storage facilities deal in certain goods that are produced in a given season that figure might be fairly high. I should also like to know whether or not the storage survey was broken down as to areas, regions or provinces because if the city of Toronto has ample cold storage facilities and is using only 40 per cent of the potential

Supply-Agriculture
capacity of the facilities this does not do much good for the people in the constituency of my friend the hon. member for Skeena if they are greatly in need of such facilities. A national average of 50 per cent occupancy does not mean very much unless it is a general pattern that is prevalent all across the country. I am wondering if the minister could say to what extent there was occupancy of cold storage facilities a few years ago and whether the survey would show by provinces that the rate of use of cold storage varies a great deal.

Mr. Chairman, we receive monthly returns as to the occupancy of these various cold storage plants and these are compiled on a yearly basis. The general trend of occupancy has been downward for some years past. In other words, the percentage of occupancy has been declining. These figures, of course, are broken down on a provincial and regional basis. There is naturally some variation on a provincial and regional basis but the chief variation is on a seasonal basis. At some seasons of the year occupancy is low and at other times it runs as high as 70 per cent in some cases, as I mentioned. Nevertheless the general trend of occupancy has been decreasing.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me this is a good example of the fact that whenever you attempt to put into effect a necessary economy, one which will save the taxpayers some money and one which serves other useful purposes, you immediately receive complaints from some hon. members of the house which makes it difficult to institute economies in government services. This is a case in which I think there is no question whatever but that the granting of subsidies running up to as much as $1 million or more to build cold storage plants is absolutely unjustified. We have sufficient cold storage facilities now. On the average it does not have more than 50 per cent occupancy. Why in the world should we continue to spend the taxpayers' money in building more cold storage facilities in the light of the situation I have outlined which would force a lot of people into bankruptcy? I cannot understand that kind of reasoning. Certainly the provision we have made of a $50,000 grant which is still available is sufficient to cover the needs of the smaller communities where storage facilities have not yet been built. The smaller areas are the only places where there is a necessity for new cold storage plants.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a few words to what I said a few moments ago with respect to the situation. I live in Saskatchewan where we have a

cold storage operation rigidly supervised by the Department of Agriculture. We have 216 licensed cold storage locker operators in that province. I believe the standard of operation is one of the best in Canada. Having been an executive officer of the governing association for some years I have watched the trend in this field.
Cold storage lockers came into popularity in Saskatchewan in about 1945. The popularity of usage increased sharply until approximately 1950. Beginning in that year there was a decline in cold storage occupancy. We as cold storage operators had educated the public to the value of cold storage and the economy of processing foods. The advent of home freezers on the consumer market lessened the need for commercial locker plants. I would presume to. say there would be possibly twice as much food in cold storage today as there was in 1945 but it is in the individual homes. The result of this is that many operators in Saskatchewan feel they are going to be faced in the not too distant future with the problem of keeping their plants fully occupied and operating economically.
I believe the minister is taking the right stand in this regard. He is following the trend that has taken place in my province and I understand the same trend has taken place right across Canada. Rural electrification is taking place in many areas and the moment it is established a home freezer is the first utility the farm wife wants. The result is that she takes her products away from commercial locker plants. I can speak with some knowledge of the situation in Regina and elsewhere because I have spoken in the last few years to the operators of plants in those areas. This is a normal trend and something to which we must face up.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think the minister has given us ample reasons why there should be this arbitrary limit. I am surprised that if he has made this comprehensive survey and the records come in from time to time he or his departmental officials who are before him do not have copies of these documents so the committee could see the entire cold storage picture across the country.
I was critical over the years of the former minister of agriculture, probably as critical as any hon. member of this house, but I was always prepared to say that as far as cold storage subsidies were concerned he was improving the program. Today we have determination on the part of the Minister of Agriculture to save money in this field and applications will not be judged on

their individual merits. We all are aware of what was pointed out by the hon. member for Moose Mountain that other facilities are being made available.
We have a minister who does not judge each case on its merits, but arbitrarily slices off any chance there is of a co-operative, or any other organization, getting a grant in excess of $50,000. I am not one of those who has spent my time asking the government to spend its time ferreting out economies; but if the government wants to make some real economies I think they can be made in some department, generally speaking, other than the Department of Agriculture because, in my opinion, expenditures in the Department of Agriculture have never been excessive.
I am wondering whether, when the minister made this survey of which he has spoken a great deal, it was a special survey or whether it was merely a reading of those annual reports that normally come in from across the country. Can the minister tell the committee the percentage of cold storages in use in this country by provinces?

Mr. Chairman, the investigation that I have made was a matter of taking those monthly reports-as I say, they are not yearly reports; we get them in monthly in regard to occupancy-and compiling the statistics. The hon. member will realize that that is a big job because there are a lot of those cold storages across Canada.
As far as judging any particular application for a cold storage on its merits is concerned, as I indicated before, that is what is done. When an application comes in a very careful investigation is made before a contract is entered into, and once more the costs which are submitted by the organization are very carefully audited and gone into before we pay out this subsidy. The thing is done on an individual basis and has always been done on an individual basis; but it seemed to me that as far as cold storage which was to be subsidized by the Canadian taxpayer, in the future, is concerned in view of the extent of the occupancy which exists at the present time and in view of the number of cold storages there are in all centres of any size, the only need for continued subsidization was in the smaller areas where cold storage has not yet been built. The limit of $50,000 I considered, and still consider, was more than ample to cover the needs of those communities. That is why the sum of $50,000 was put in as our contribution, which means a cold storage costing $150,000.
As far as the break-down of figures by provinces is concerned, the hon. member 57071-3-187*
Supply-Agriculture
realizes that it is a big job. I have this book here which is just a summary of the various details, as far as these estimates are concerned, and it is an absolute impossibility to have here all of the documents which might be asked for. As far as information is concerned, such as the break-down of those cold storages, the officials just could not carry the documents. As I said before to the hon. member for Skeena, I will be glad to get the break-down by provinces, and so forth, but I have not it here at the present time, and it is just not feasible to have everything along with me here when I am taking up my estimates, as I think the hon. member realizes.

Mr. Chairman, there was another way in which the minister could have attained his objective if his objective was to save money or to accomplish economies. He could have taken each application and looked at it on its merits to see whether or not in a given locality such new cold storage facilities were needed. If in the opinion of the minister they were not needed, then it would not be necessary to grant a subsidy. My point is, if a co-operative wishes to build a cold storage plant, if it is needed, at a cost of $600,000, then it is a retrograde step to say that this co-operative is not able to get $200,000 by way of a grant but can only get $50,000. There were other ways of bringing about the same result, if that result were desired, other than to say that $50,000 is the limit and there will be no other subsidization of cold storage accommodation provided in this country. I do not think you can build anything adequate with the present building costs for the sum of $150,000. I would say that would be a relatively small plant at present costs.

1 think the hon. member has forgotten what were the purpose and the intent of the Cold Storage Act. Its purpose and intent were to provide cold storages which were deficient in number at the time the act was passed, and it was a subsidy by the Canadian taxpayer to encourage people to put up cold storages because there was not anything like enough cold storages in existence. Now once you reach the point where you have sufficient cold storages over the country so that they are only 50 per cent occupied surely the need for any subsidy has disappeared. As I say, I would have done away with the subsidy entirely; I would have asked to have the act repealed except for the fact that in quite a considerable number of those more isolated areas there is still a need for the construction of many of those smaller cold storages, and that is why the limit of $50,000 was put in.

Supply-Agriculture
Furthermore, I might say this. Any concern which is going to build a cold storage costing more than $150,000 should be able to raise the money itself. If the cold storage is going to be sufficiently profitable, well, then, they should be able to raise the money themselves; they should not need any subsidy from the Canadian taxpayer in building it. If there was a definite shortage, as existed at one time, well and good, the subsidy was justified; but when you have a situation where you have only a 50 per cent occupancy of those cold storages, then, in my opinion, it is completely unjustifiable to ask the Canadian taxpayer to put up money to build more of them. The result of building more of them, in most instances, is just to put out of business or into bankruptcy concerns which already have them.

I realize the minister may not have this information before him or it may be difficult to find, but can he indicate what the results of this survey showed with respect to percentage of occupancy of fish cold storage plants in Prince Rupert, and whether there is or is not a deficiency of them?
I can send that information to the hon. member. As I said, naturally I have not it here.
I am sorry; I was trying to listen to two people at the same time.
I said that I can send him that information but naturally I have not it here.
Did the minister compile that information as a result of a survey?

I do not know what the hon. member is asking me, whether we compiled the information. We have the complete figures as to the occupancy month by month of those various cold storages, and from that information, which takes up a great deal of room in the files, we can compile any information which is asked for. But what is compiled at the present time and what I can lay my finger on in 10 minutes or half an hour I do not know.

Well, what I am trying to get at in another way and to point out is that I think this is an incorrect way of approaching this problem and saying that because we have discovered from the results of the Canada-wide study an average percentage use of cold storages is made, therefore that average should apply to every place. Some may be above and some below. I say that is an inequitable use of the results. To apply it all across the board

and I do not want to put words in the minister's mouth-is to say

that Prince Rupert does not need additional cold storage facilities without knowing whether that is so or not.

All I can say is this. I have explained several times before, and I have to take the responsibility, that in my opinion there is no need for the subsidization of cold storage facilities anywhere in the country in excess of $50,000 per cold storage plant. That is my opinion and I have to be responsible for the decision. I have taken it and I do not think I can say anything further about the matter. From the information I have received I am convinced that there are sufficient large cold storage plants in all of the more populous areas of the country, that further subsidization of them is not required and not only is not required but simply has the effect of damaging already established cold storage plants and organizations.
I am appreciative of the fact that the minister has just indicated there is no need for subsidization with respect to fish cold storage facilities in Prince Rupert.
I did not say that.
In effect.
I said that in my opinion $50,000 was ample by way of subsidy.

The minister is saying that $50,000 is an ample subsidy to meet what the act was originally intended to meet, a deficiency in cold storage facilities, and he is saying that without having any knowledge of the conditions existing in Prince Rupert.

All I can say is that we cannot pass special legislation in the case of one cold storage plant out of hundreds or thousands in the country which happens to be located in Prince Rupert or anywhere else.

I suggest that the minister can pass regulations which will give him the authority to look at these matters on the merits of each individual case and adjust the subsidy, if necessary, just as is done by the government in many other actions it takes.

How much of this money is for economic research to help farmers improve the efficiency of their farms from the point of view of business operation? Is this information available to farmers?

Could we have an explanation of the grants and other assistance, how they are spread around and to whom?

These grants for the consolidation and improvement of cheese factories have been in effect for quite a number of years. Up to now I think the majority of cheese factories have had subsidies paid to them at some time or other. At the present time most of the subsidies are paid in cases where you have in the same area or just a few miles apart two or three old cheese factories or a co-operative or the owner of one of these cheese factories wants to consolidate his operations into a larger and more modern factory. He applies for a grant for that purpose. In the same way as we do with respect to cold storage we investigate the matter and if it is justified, if there seems to be a need, it is approved and a contract is entered into. In this case the subsidy is 50 per cent of the cost of the improvement or consolidation as the case may be. Quite frequently you have a case where a combination factory is being erected, one designed to manufacture cheese in one part and butter in another. The grant is only made for that part which is devoted to the manufacture of cheese.
I understood the minister to say that the amount is 50 per cent of the total cost as related to cheese.
Yes.
Is it a subsidy?
Yes, it is a subsidy.
Is there any justification for applying the same theory or principle in this case as in the case of cold storage facilities?

To begin with, the amounts of subsidy paid out are nothing like the amounts which have been paid out in the

Supply-Agriculture
case of cold storage facilities. Ordinarily the amounts are relatively small. The general purpose of this is to improve the cheese making facilities and therefore the quality of the cheese, which I think is still essential because we are only now able to sell the best quality cheese.

I notice that there is an amount of $128,923 shown as a decrease under this item, and I would like the assurance of the minister that he is not going to commence to do away with part of these subsidies. My hon. friends can take advantage of my experience in this respect in that the 50 per cent grant is more important than the subsidy for cold storage.
This measure was instituted by the Liberal government and the work they did was first class, and that is why Canadian cheese is recognized as the best produced in the world. The subsidies made it possible for the cheese makers to buy the best machinery and the best facilities with which to keep it in good condition. I do not agree, therefore, with my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture that this amount should be decreased.
In my own village a man had to apply for a subsidy to build a larger building. This was not permitted at that time but it was urgent that he do this job. He was receiving 100,000 pounds of milk per day and he is now receiving 210,000 pounds of milk per day. Anyone who knows anything about milk will realize that 210,000 pounds of milk is "some milk". It was necessary for him to do this work immediately so that the farmers would have a place to which they might deliver their milk and when in this country we are talking about helping farming we refer to amelioration of conditions and the overcoming of our difficulties. We should therefore be increasing rather than decreasing the subsidies.
The Liberal government did a good job and I am hoping that the cabinet will help my good friend the Minister of Agriculture. I know him well enough to know that he wishes to do a good job and I ask every member on the government side to help him out, not here but in caucus. I hope they will get the Minister of Finance to give him the money he needs for we must increase help to the farmers of our country along with the manufacturers of other products. The conditions in the agricultural industry, especially over the last 25 years, have been quite different from those in any other industry. It is not the same thing at all. There is an increase or amelioration of 300 per cent in respect of assistance to other industries and I ask the minister not to forget what I asked him in a friendly way, that he should not

But it is not their desire to come back to the house again, and that is why they are asking at this time for $25 million, to be able to issue debentures and bonds to that extent. As I got the information from the bridge authority, what they are requesting now is that this be passed authorizing them to issue debentures and bonds to the extent of $25 million which they hope they will have to issue only to the extent of $22 million.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I last spoke on the floor of the house on the question of capital punishment I have been doing some research into what type of person kills, into the types who may repeat a killing and into the history of the effectiveness of the death penalty as a deterrent to murder. On the other occasion I expressed the opinion that the death penalty should not be abolished through the motion of a private member but rather that if such action were to be taken it should be only after full and complete study by a committee

Criminal Code
of this house and the other place. The further research I have done has served to strengthen that first opinion.
I have found in my research that persons who kill can usually be fitted into two principal categories. There is first the cold, premeditated killer who plans his killing long in advance, who attempts to foresee every possible weakness in his plan and who hopes by careful planning to make his crime impossible of solution.
This type of killer usually kills for a definite purpose. He may kill for revenge. He may kill for monetary gain. He may wish to attain power. He always has a motive and once that motive has been achieved-with the exception of course of professional gang killers-he rarely kills again. Such killers when detected almost invariably receive the death sentence and in most cases the sentence is carried out.
The second type is, of course, the emotional killer. He may kill for a variety of reasons. It may be jealousy. It may be a fancied wrong. The slightest thing as trivial as a badly cooked dinner can set off a spark that will result in death. Drinking has also played a part in many such slayings. The majority of such persons are considered legally sane. That is, they have the ability to distinguish between right and wrong and accordingly are fit to stand trial for murder. But I suggest to this house that their emotional instability is such that they may be completely unable to control their actions. It is in such people that the danger of repeat killings lies.
Yet it would seem that the law leans heavily in favour of these emotionally unstable persons. Almost invariably the verdict in such cases is manslaughter. The sentence may be 10 years. It may be less or it may be more but it is a foregone conclusion that in a comparatively short period they will be turned loose again on society, those emotionally unstable people and who can say, if the same set of circumstances arise, that is, if the dinner is burned or if the wife stays out too late at night, or if they again have a few more drinks than they are able to handle, the same people will not kill again? Statistics indicate that the danger exists. These statistics also indicate that the man who commits a premeditated murder, and who does not pay with his life for the killing, rarely commits another crime. In England, over a period of 50 years, there was only one case of such a convicted murderer repeating his crime. In fact, records show that the majority of such people, after attaining their freedom, become good, responsible citizens.
It is because of these things that I say the question of capital punishment-whether
[Mr. Rynard.l
it should be retained or abolished-is not something that can be decided lightly by a snap vote in this house.
Who are those people who might be classified as emotional killers? In my opinion, the best survey that I have been able to find is one made by the state of Wisconsin. Strangely enough, this survey would indicate that the path toward killing often began when the killer was still a child, and that in many cases much of the blame rested with the parents. In seven cases out of 10 these emotional killers came from an unfavourable family background. In about 40 per cent of the cases, for instance, either one or both of the parents were alcoholics. In 60 per cent of the cases the child was out earning money before the age of 14 and contributing to the family budget. In 90 per cent of the cases they were making their contribution before they had reached the age of 18 years. It is not surprising, therefore, that the vast majority of those emotional murderers were found to be people who had left school at an extremely early age and who had no opportunity to learn either a trade or a profession.
In 50 per cent of the cases the killer had not as a child been conscious of the love of either his mother or his father, and indeed the feeling of rejection was stronger in at least 20 per cent of those cases who said they hated their parents. Nervous instability is always a very strong factor. Again, in one-fifth of the cases, the killer came from a family where there was a history of insanity, epilepsy, or some other emotional disturbance.
The over-all result of this survey also is interesting, for the statistics indicate that one out of every four people who kill is insane, one out of every four is an alcoholic and one out of every three cases had an I.Q. of below 70 per cent. Unfortunately, there appear to be no such statistics available in Canada, but it is the sort of information that I believe is essential to any full and effective study of the question of capital punishment. I believe that such a survey should be attempted.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me to be at least somewhat anomalous that we should be here discussing the fate of an individual in view of the situation in the world today. This afternoon the world is divided into two armed camps capable of mass murder and legal slaughter, but we in this house are spending some hours discussing a measure that concerns only an individual and can affect at most only the occasional person in our population. And perhaps, in this very fact that we can discuss capital punishment while the world faces the horrible prospects of

war lies the great hope for democracy as we in Canada believe in it, and the best chance of freedom for people now enslaved by ideologies abhorrent to us in this house. But it is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that the nations of the world, while uttering lip service to the humanities have not become less cruel with the passing of time. Indeed the history of the world and the history of killing are so closely related that the history of one is almost the history of the other. We are almost forced to the conclusion that man has shown greater ingenuity in inventing and perfecting methods and machines for killing his fellow man than in any other pursuit.
Had the money devoted to the development of the atomic and hydrogen bomb been used in medical research I wonder whether we would not long since have found a cure for cancer, for multiple sclerosis, for muscular dystrophy and those other conditions which still, in far too many cases, mean death and a more certain death than the legal sentence of a court that a man shall be hanged by the neck or strapped in an electric chair, or placed in a metal cylinder with a dish of acid and a cyanide pellet to kill him. I wonder, too, whether, ironically enough, we do not find in today's international situation the ultimate example of the effectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent to murder.
After world war II the western powers, the victors, decided that in the years to come men must never again embark on war; there must be before such men the threat and the fear of personal punishment. Therefore, it was decided to seek out those Germans whom the western powers believed responsible for the last war and to bring them to trial. Hitler, the author of the conflict, escaped through death by his own hand in a Berlin bunker. Goebbels, another of the arch conspirators, went with him; but the majority of the others were rounded up. An international court of justice was set up at Nuremberg. The accused were given the protection of the western concept of law. They were faced by their accusers. They heard the evidence against them. They had the opportunity of putting in their defence. Day after day the proceedings went on. Day after day thousands of words went out to the newspapers of the world. Never was a trial attended by so much publicity. In the end what happened? Twenty-two high-ranking Nazis were convicted of war crimes. Eleven were sentenced to death. With the exception of Herman Goering, who evaded the hangman by use of a secreted cyanide pellet, they went to their deaths in a mass execution, at which the world, through press, radio and films, occupied a ringside seat.

Has the death by hanging of those 10 topranking Nazis as the result of the action of the international court of justice been a deterrent to international crime? I have my own opinion of course, but Mr. Nasser, Mr. Khrushchev and Mr. Stalin, if he were available, would be more competent witnesses than I.
There is one other aspect of this matter of capital punishment that I believe merits some attention. Respect for law in general is the foundation of our whole system of democracy under which neighbour is able to live peacefully with neighbour. In this connection I wonder, should the government decide to set up a parliamentary committee to study this whole matter of capital punishment, whether one of the directions to that committee should not be to make a study of public opinion on capital punishment? When I say "public opinion" I mean just that. I do not mean the officials and the lawyers of the crown; I do not mean only the psychiatrists, the penologists and the welfare workers; I mean plain John Doe who is quite likely some day to find himself a member of a jury trying somebody for murder.
I make this suggestion because my study of the effectiveness of capital punishment has made one thing clear to me. In my previous remarks on this matter I mentioned that there was a time in the United Kingdom when more than 100 crimes were punishable by death. Members may be of the opinion that it was the professionals, the lawyers, the parliamentarians, the crown officials, who cut that vast total down to the comparatively few that remain today, but I differ because I firmly believe that it was the plain Jones, Smiths and Browns who sat on these cases as jurors who forced the change. With their power they refused to bring in verdicts where the law said that the crime merited death. Their constant refusal to convict in capital offences was, in my opinion, one of the great factors in bringing about moderation in the British concept of justice.
I do not intend to interpret what is in the minds of the men who make up the juries in Canadian courts of criminal law today, but it does seem to me that there is an increasing tendency to bring in a verdict of manslaughter when even 10 or 15 years ago the same set of facts would have resulted in a verdict of murder and probable death by hanging. It seems to me that there would be a great deal of merit in studying the facts of the so-called murders of recent years and the verdicts of the juries who were best acquainted with these facts. Out of such a study I think a pattern would emerge that would be the best indication of the actual thinking of the Canadian people today.

Criminal Code
With such information before us I believe that we could place a measure of punishment on our statute books that the Canadian people more nearly believed to be fitted to the crime. By doing so we would increase respect not only for the law as it applies to murder but also for all laws, respect for which is so essential to Canadian community living.

speechtext:
In any event, I find it
somewhat surprising that this group now pales at the old historic process of British hanging. I have always believed, as I believe now and as I think I will always conscientiously believe, that the hangman is an influence for good. I have formed that conclusion over a number of years-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member thinks the hangman should also be the prosecutor.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
As a practising lawyer I have acted for the defence in capital cases, and I have also prosecuted for the crown in capital cases. In my province this year we are celebrating our centenary and in some of the publicity about it, in dealing with our history, some misguided persons have referred to the late Chief Justice Sir Matthew Baillie Begbie as the hanging judge.
Sir Matthew Baillie Begbie was no more a hanging judge than any other judge; judges are only hanging judges because they must pronounce the sentences provided by the criminal law of Canada. I want to refer in the course of my argument to one way in which that long since deceased judge was able to effectively influence a large group of people. This incident occurred many years ago during the Fraser river gold rush at the then city of Yale where some 2,000 unruly miners who were in the habit of wandering around fully armed, usually carrying two guns and a bandolier of shells-they were not British Columbians for the most part-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext: C.C.F.'ers?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
When the chief justice
arrived in Yale with the British Columbia police chief-and in those days the British Columbia police consisted of one man, Chief Chartres Brew-there was rowdyism going on, but the chief of police managed to get order. The chief justice got up on a stump, and with his rather stern visage, surveyed this group of rather lawless individuals and, having obtained order, he said "Now, gentlemen-" -I think he was very kind_____________"I
just want to make one observation, and that is this, if there is a shooting I can assure you there will be a hanging." That had a great effect amongst that group of lawless people and there were very very few capital cases in that area.
I would like to speak for a moment or two on my experience in the courts of law in

Criminal Code
regard to capital cases. When one acts for the defence in a capital case one is always nervous and there is a great deal of tension involved, but I must admit that I cannot remember ever thinking or hoping that because of this nervousness and tension the sentence of hanging should be abolished. That has never entered my mind. In prosecuting for the crown one is in a different position; there is not the same responsibility or duty on the prosecutor for the crown. He must not struggle for conviction-we simply produce the evidence and the verdict of the jury is what governs. It is not and it never has been under our system of criminal jurisprudence easy to get a conviction for murder.
I can think of one instance in the year 1944 when I conducted an assize for the crown in the city of Vancouver, and on the docket we had four murder cases. There was one conviction and one hanging; there was one acquittal and there were two manslaughter verdicts. One man got a fairly heavy sentence and the other a fairly light sentence.
I think most practising lawyers will agree that this is about the average for these cases.
I know, and this is confirmed in the joint committee report of 1956, that there are those who think innocent men may be hanged, but I think this possibility is very remote. Those of us who practise in the courts of Canada know that with all the protection that a British court of justice places around an accused person-and this I conscientiously believe-it is almost impossible for an innocent man to be found guilty of murder and subsequently hanged.
We also have those who refer to the horror of the hanging itself. It must after all be remembered, however, that a hanging only follows a conviction and while it may be said that it is a horrible affair and a degrading affair, murder is also a degrading affair. I think we must keep in our minds the proper perspective of the conviction and the subsequent hanging. Once there is a conviction of murder the subsequent hanging is something with which we do not need to concern ourselves too much.
In the report of the joint committee of 1956 it was pointed out-and I think this is very significant-that in every case the law enforcement officers of the provinces, with the sole exception of Saskatchewan, were of the opinion that the death sentence for murder should be retained.
As I said in opening my remarks, my experience has led me to believe that the hangman is an influence for good. We are, after all, dealing with murder and we need not worry about cases of homicide committed in a moment of passion because a British

jury will never bring in a verdict of murder there-that is manslaughter. We need not worry about cases of justifiable homicide because they result in acquittal. My experience is not as large as that of some others, but I believe you only get a verdict of guilty from a British jury when it is a case of cold-blooded murder and I contend that if it is a case of cold-blooded murder the hangman has his proper place and it is a good thing for the country that this system exists.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in a rather curious position in disagreeing with practically everything that has been said by a member of my own party and agreeing substantially with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). This is one of those rare occasions on which I think we agree. I agree with him to the extent that I do not think the deterrent aspect of capital punishment can be established. I have received the reports of the joint Senate and Commons committee on capital punishment and of the royal commission in Great Britain. Nothing in that evidence has led me to the conclusion that the deterrent aspect can be upheld. The same thing goes for the arguments advanced with regard to the protection of the police. For other reasons I reject out of hand the attempts to relate statistics, in terms of their unreliability, saying for example that 15.9 murders occurred per 100,000 people in certain areas and comparing that figure with the figures for certain other areas.
In my opinion the factors at work to bring about the conditions leading to murder cannot be simply put through an I.B.M. machine and an effective argument produced. Arguing from the point of view that capital punishment should be abolished, I should like to say that in my opinion I do not think our legal system as presently constituted or as it is expected to be changed can reach a sufficiently certain conclusion to justify the taking of a man's life. A man's life is something far more important than any other factor or than any other event that can occur in any of our lives.
Let us look at the situation concerning the structure of the law and what is involved in the trial. We have the judge and his attitude and influence. If he has certain tendencies which would tend to prejudice his position and direct the attention of the jury to a verdict of guilty of murder, how can those tendencies be detected? If they are detected, how can they be corrected under our present system? Yet I believe that in some cases this attitude on the part of judges exists. My friend the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. McPhillips) mentioned prosecutors. Prosecutors in

the main have considerable experience in the treatment of such cases. They can bring to them background, they have experienced assistants and facilities to gather a prodigious amount of evidence.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext: Leading to conviction?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext: Not necessarily; and here we are disagreeing again. On the other hand the defence, in the case where the defendant is not a rich man or if a cause celebre is not involved, is most likely to end up with legal aid and in that case, I submit, with a counsel who is not as experienced as is his counterpart the prosecutor. From my observation, my readings and my research in this matter, I am led to believe that in the great majority of cases the odds are loaded against the defendant in a murder trial on that basis alone. Then we come to the jury and I can speak with some more authority, if you like, in this regard, having served on two consecutive murder juries a few years ago.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext: Did you convict?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, for the record, in both cases we did bring in a guilty of murder verdict. In both cases the guilty of murder verdict was appealed. In both cases the verdict was disallowed and the appeal was granted on the basis of misdirection on the part of the judge. In one case the charge was reduced to manslaughter in a subsequent trial, I believe, and in the second case the man was committed as being insane. Yet within that framework, within the framework of the law and the structure of the law as it exists and as it was put to us, there was virtually no alternative to the verdict which we in fact brought in.
But there are other aspects of this matter of the jury that I think bear discussion and mention here. One is the presence of people of sadistic inclination. I can draw no other conclusion from the result of a jury vote, having acted as foreman of the jury. When the votes and slips and paper were handed to me at a certain stage of our deliberations I found that one of the members of the jury had drawn a sketch of a man hanging from a scaffold. Does that indicate a normal and reasonable attitude to this subject on the part of the juror? There is the question of the ability of jurors, on the basis of the selection presently carried out, to cope with the complicated medical and psychiatric evidence where you have, as happened in one case, three and four psychiatrists offering authoritative medical opinion. During the greater part of that time a substantial percentage of the jury were not aware of what any of those doctors were talking about. They all reached
Criminal Code
a different conclusion, all for some excellent and impressive sounding medical reasons.
The other story, of course, bespeaks attitudes of the men who get to be jurors. I simply offer one example to indicate an approach taken. One of the cases involved an Italian immigrant who had been involved in a knifing. The attitude expressed by one of these jurors was: "I think we should hang him as an example to any other immigrants coming into this country". I do not believe this attitude, this frame of mind, has any place in the consideration, under our system of justice, as to whether a man is guilty or not guilty or whether he should or should not be hanged.
If I may have one moment beyond six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that capital punishment cannot be abolished. Last week we were told in Toronto that a certain packing company has erected a device for disposing of pigs, something which cost them $50,000. This step was largely as a result of effort by humane-minded people to bring about the humane slaughter of pigs. I suggest that if the manner in which we are now executing people found guilty of murder were proposed as a method of disposing of or slaughtering food animals in any slaughter house in this country we would have something approaching revolution on our hands. May I move the adjournment of the debate.
