Supply-Agriculture AFTER RECESS
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
41. To provide lor administrative expenses, Agricultural Stabilization Act, $88,390.

Mr. Chairman, immediately before we adjourned for the private members hour, the hon. member for Welland had asked a series of questions. First, he wanted to have me put on record the different price supports that are established for different vegetables. I have that information here. There are soybeans which are supported at $2.10 a bushel and sugar beets which are supported on a differential basis according to what the prices have been, as laid down by the stabilization act-the average price over the last 10 years. The support price in Alberta is .0099 cents, in Manitoba, .0938 cents, in Ontario, .0798 cents and the same in Quebec. Tomatoes are supported, choice in case, at $5.20 a case; asparagus, Ontario No. 1, 18 cents a pound in Ontario factories and 17 cents a pound at British Columbia factories. Those are the vegetables that are supported.
The hon. member also asked whether, if a price support is established very much below the market price, it does not gravitate down to or near the price support level. If that is the situation I would point out the example of hogs. Hogs have been supported for several years at $23 a hundred. They have varied in price, going up to $35 during that period. At the present time they are supported at $25 a hundred and the present price, as I recall it, on the Toronto and Montreal markets is around $32 a hundred. I think that is an example of the fact that you can have a support price and it does not become a ceiling price, which I think is what was in the hon. member's mind.
These are the questions that I have that the hon. member mentioned. He said something about asparagus. He said: "I know that in the Niagara district that happened in the case of asparagus. For instance, in 1950 asparagus was selling from 224 cents a pound to 23 cents a pound. I do not know what it was selling for in 1950-"
Pardon me, but I said 1956.

Then the hon. member goes on to say: "In 1957 the price fell about a cent, and when it fell about a cent, members of the minister's party infiltrated among the asparagus-" I do not know anything about any members of my party having infiltrated into the Niagara area. Certainly, I did not send anyone round there, and unlike some of his political associates I have
[The Chairman.]
no goon squads, and have never had any. With regard to the remainder of the questions which the hon. member asked, I have not got the sheet and I cannot recall them. Perhaps the hon. member would like to ask his questions over.
Could you tell us the support prices on fruits?

The only support price is on raspberries which, packed in S02, are supported at 144 cents a pound at British Columbia factories and in frozen form at 15 cents. This is not fresh fruit. It is put up in S02.

I had occasion to spend the morning and the afternoon in the veterans affairs committee, so I have not been very much of a nuisance to the minister today but I do rise on this item to bring briefly to the attention of the committee the situation of the British Columbia fruit growers, because I find some misunderstanding and failure on the part of many members of the public in general to realize their need for assistance and the modest nature of the request put forward by the British Columbia fruit growers.
I was advised that about the middle of June they made certain submissions to the stabilization board asking for differential payments for certain tree fruits, and they wanted those submissions to receive the earliest attention as the industry was awaiting the outcome with great anxiety. They also informed me that they would regard this as an indication of the government's intention in the field of price support. I presume that they supplied a number of hon. members with their submission to the board regarding the British Columbia apple crop, 1957, and so on. I will quote briefly from this submission to indicate clearly to hon. members the position of the fruit growers with respect to the 1957 crop.
Before doing that I want to quote the paragraphs in the brief dealing with the cost of production of a packed box of apples and the same applies to the cost of production with regard to other tree fruits in respect of which they have asked for deficiency payments. The submission in this respect reads as follows:
We have based our estimate of the cost of producing a box of apples on statistics provided by a Canada Department of Agriculture publication called "A Study of Apple Production in the Okanagan Valley of British Columbia 1949", a report of a survey of 153 Okanagan Valley orchards conducted by D. W. Ware, E, D. Woodward and H. W. Trevor during the years 1948-49.
You can see that they arrived at the figures for the cost of production of these various

tree fruits on the basis of information contained in a recognized government statistical survey.
With respect to apples they had this to say, and I am simply going to give the summary of their conclusions in each case so that hon. members will be informed of the seriousness of the situation. The summary with respect to apples is as follows:
The foregoing we believe reveals that B.C. Tree Fruits Limited, under extreme difficulties succeeded in disposing of the whole apple crop produced within the area under the jurisdiction of the Natural Products Marketing (British Columbia) Act. The average net return per box of apples to the producer was 87 cents and the estimated cost of producing a box was $1.79. The final out-turn on the season's operations of producing and marketing the B.C. apple crop was an average net loss to the grower of 92 cents per box.
I believe that clearly indicates the position of the apple growers in British Columbia with respect to the 1957 crop. I turn now to the apricot crop. Again I will read the summary from the brief to save the time of the committee and to put the facts before hon. members. The submission in this respect reads as follows:
The estimated return per ton to the producer on the 1957 apricot crop will not exceed $69.58, whereas the estimated cost of production per ton was $137.61, leaving a net loss on the season's operation of $68.03 per ton.
That shows the position of the apricot growers and the need for something to be done not only to provide some assistance in the form of deficiency payments for the 1957 crop but the need for something to be done by this government to ensure that the situation is not repeated in future years as a result, shall I say, of unfair competition from certain sources.
I turn now to the question of crabapples. The summary reads as follows:
The average net return per box of crabapples to the producer in 1957 was an estimated 62 cents and the estimated cost of producing a box was $1.79. The final out-turn on the season's operations of producing and marketing the British Columbia crabapple crop was an average net loss to the grower of $1.17 per box.
That, I believe, clearly indicates the position of the growers who were producing crabapples although that tonnage is not high in relation to apples and some of the other crops.
I come now to peaches. The peach growers in south Okanagan and in some sections of my riding have been facing a difficult problem. The summary in the submission in this respect reads as follows:
The average estimated net return per ton of peaches to the grower in 1957 amounts to $76.04 against an estimated cost of production of $116.85 per ton, leaving a net loss to the producer of $40.81.
Supply-Agriculture
It can be seen that the same situation exists with respect to peach growers as exists with respect to the growers of apples, crabapples and apricots.
We turn now to the final crop for which some assistance is requested and that is prunes. The summary in this respect reads as follows:
The average estimated net return per ton of prunes in 1957 was $46.14 to the producer against an estimated cost of production of $96.81 per ton, leaving a net loss to the producer of $50.67 per ton.
I have quoted briefly from this submission. I am sure the minister is very well informed of the position of growers with respect to the 1957 crop. Mind you, the greater proportion of these growers are in the Okanagan district but on their behalf I urge that serious consideration be given to their representations which in my opinion are extremely modest indeed in relation to the net loss they have suffered on these various tree fruits. Consequently I urge the minister to make the long expected announcement in this respect as soon as possible because they are all on edge out in British Columbia awaiting word from the minister in this connection.

Mr. Chairman, I have always had a very great admiration for the command of English and the precision of word usage on the part of the hon. member for Kootenay West and therefore I was somewhat shocked when he started out by saying he was going to indicate the very modest nature of the request of the British Columbia fruit growers. The hon. member should consult the Oxford shorter dictionary or better still the full edition as to the definition of the word "modest". If he were to do that I doubt very much if he would argue that it is a term that can be properly applied to the requests of the British Columbia fruit growers in respect of the 1957 crop.
If I recall correctly their request was for a subsidy or whatever you may wish to call it in the neighbourhood of $7.4 million which is about as much as the entire fruit crop sold for and I can hardly look upon that as being properly described as modest.
I do not wish to engage in any discussion or argument with the hon. member concerning the extremely complex and difficult situation which exists as far as fruit production in British Columbia is concerned.
Why not?

If you take the figures
produced by the cost of production survey made in 1949 which served as the basis of computation for the figures produced by the British Columbia fruit growers and then apply the index figure for the cost of goods and

Supply-Agriculture
services in 1949 you still get a price of not much more than $1 for a box of apples and it may even be less. I do not suggest that this calculation gives you a correct figure but I used it for the purpose of this illustration. The figure of $1 is a long way from the figure of $1.79 which I believe was the figure referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay West. It runs in my mind that this was the figure the British Columbia fruit growers arrived at as representing their cost of production.
I must say that when cost of production figures are presented to me it does not serve any very good purpose if the figures are out of line and in fact it serves to operate in the reverse because it makes me look with grave suspicion on the whole submission. When you are given what can only be described as a fantastic figure which purports to represent the cost of production of a product it inclines you to examine the whole submission with very great care.
I regret that it has not been possible to announce whatever may or may not be done with respect to the 1957 British Columbia apple crop prior to this time. I do not have with me the file on this matter but in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West I placed on the record the date on which we received from the British Columbia growers the request for assistance with regard to the fruit crop. We wrote asking for further information in regard to the apple crop and it was finally received about ten days ago. We have been considering the matter since it was received. It has not yet been possible-for one reason, namely that, as the hon. member knows, I was away from here some five days preceding last Wednesday and necessarily so-I regret to say, to make a definite determination in regard to this matter prior to this date but I expect it will be done in the very near future.
Briefly, in reply to the minister, last evening the minister in reply to a certain statement I made said "I am a very modest person." I use the word "modest" in exactly the same sense.
You asked me whether I had not been hiding my light under a bushel.

When one reads the whole story of the requests from the British Columbia fruit growers association for assistance from the federal government over the years,
I think it is quite fair to say that their requests have been very modest indeed. The assistance given to the British Columbia fruit growers association to date for a box of apples produced in British Columbia since

assistance was first given is, as the minister knows, only a fraction of a cent a box.
Anyway, in conclusion, I do hope that the minister reaches his decision as soon as possible and I am quite confident, knowing the officers of this association for a good many years, they did present a submission which, based on facts, justifies serious consideration by this government.

I note with pleasure that the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand is acting as chairman of this committee. It is very appropriate when we are discussing an agriculture estimate. Has the Minister of Agriculture the figures available as to exports and imports between Canada and the United States with respect to the apple crop of both countries?

We have not those figures here, Mr. Chairman, but I can say roughly- this is confirmed by my officials here-that over the past 10 years we have exported about twice as many apples to the United States as we have imported from them.
It may not be appropriate on this item, but would the minister consider it and give me in somewhat broad terms the relationship of the exports and imports with respect to potatoes?
If the hon. member would wait a moment the officials think that perhaps they can look it up. We can go on with something else and I will come back and answer it.
Has the minister any figures as to amounts paid out under the Agricultural Stabilization Act?

Mr. Chairman, there was tabled in the house a short time ago a report of the operations of the Agricultural Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Prices Support Act for the end of the last fiscal year. Most of that was in connection with the Agricultural Prices Support Act, because the stabilization act came into effect only on March 1, so there is only a month of the stabilization act figures in that report. We have really no figures that I can give the hon. gentleman as to the cost of operations since that time. I might say that most of the operations have been purchase operations. We have purchased various commodities and we have not yet resold them; therefore we do not know what the cost will be. The other operations are ones in which we have guaranteed a deficiency payment. In other words, we have guaranteed a certain support price and if the commodity is sold at less than that support price we will make up the difference. We have not had any results of the sales yet, therefore we have

not paid out anything under those programs. As a result I am not in a position to give any figures as to what the cost has been up to the present time.

Can the minister give the committee some idea of those commodities which are now being supported at prices higher than the current market price? I would think that in regard to hogs, steers and lambs the support price is so much lower than the market price that it is not likely the floor price will be paid during the present year. I would like to know what commodities are being supported at the present time at prices below the market price and what commodities are being supported at prices higher than the market, and what commodities are being purchased? The minister referred to some commodities which are now being purchased and that other commodities have support prices.
I think we can get some idea, at any rate, as to what commodities in fact are likely to have some real support under this act.

To begin with, Mr. Chairman, only one of those commodities under the stabilization act has real support under it. I am glad to say that so far as the majority of those commodities is concerned, the present market price is above the support price.
Every product.

No, not every product. In the majority of products it is above the support price. The hon. member for Assiniboia mentioned cattle, sheep and hogs. I might say there is a great deal of, we will say, perturbation amongst a large number of hog men to whom I have spoken in the past month as to whether the price will not go down to the support price this fall. I sincerely hope that it does not go down to the support price, but nevertheless, as I say, there is a great deal of fear on the part of a large number of hog producers that that will be the situation and they are extremely glad that the support price is at $25 a hundred rather than at $23 a hundred.
As to the specific question of what commodities are supported above the market price, they are butter, cheese, skim milk, wool and, until very recently, eggs. Eggs are now, I am glad to say, above the support price; but all of these commodities have been or are above the ordinary market price; that is, the support price is above the ordinary market price and we are buying them as a result of that.

For example, butter is supported at 64 cents a pound. Can the minister tell us how much that is above the market price?
Supply-Agriculture

Naturally, as the hon.
gentleman knows, if we are buying butter at 64 cents, that keeps it at 64 cents. It is not allowed to fall below 64 cents. If there was no support price there I do not like to venture to predict what the price of butter would be, but I know it would be a great deal lower. The hon. member knows that butter is selling in London, England, probably the greatest world market there is for butter, at 23 cents a pound.

We have just passed the first third of the fiscal year for obligations under this act. Has the minister any estimate of gain or loss or whether we are ahead or behind with regard to the act in the first third of the current fiscal year?

It is impossible to be ahead from a financial point of view as far as this act is concerned. Any estimate that would be made would be an estimate of how much was paid out under the act, and that is the type of estimate which I think the hon. gentleman realizes it is impossible to make. If the general world price of eggs, for example, drops to 50 per cent of what it is at the present time our obligations with respect to eggs are going to be very heavy but if the general world price of eggs remains at about what it is at the present time and we do not have terrific overproduction of eggs-
Eggs are above the support price.

They are at the moment. They were not until about a week or two ago. I just take that as an example. If we do not have a big over-production of eggs in Canada then the cost will not be too great, and the same thing applies to every other commodity. If the general price at which hogs can be exported to the United States fell below $25 a hundred then our obligations under this act would again become very heavy but as long as we can still export a certain amount of pork to the United States and their price remains about at the level it is now we are not going to have to pay anything under the stabilization act. As I say, this applies to every commodity. It depends entirely on how the general outside market for goods goes and what the supply of those goods is in Canada during the particular season.

I can quite understand that the Minister of Agriculture would not be able to tell us, for instance, [DOT] what the relative holdings of products under stabilization prices were as of yesterday, which was the end of the fourth month of the current fiscal year, but perhaps as of a month ago

Supply-Agriculture
he might be able to tells us in relation to the previous year what were the stocks of the products that it was necessary to purchase under the price stabilization act.

We have quite a list of stocks. I understand the hon. member wants the stocks we hold at the present time compared with the stocks held at some previous time. The stocks held at the present time are as follows-
What date?

July 25. Butter is roughly 59 million pounds. It is split into four different types of butter but when they are added together it comes to roughly 59 million pounds. With respect to dry skim milk, spray process, 1957-58 purchases up to May 1>
1958, were 14,801,000 pounds and 1958 purchases after May 1, 1958 were 24,362,000 pounds or a total of 39 million pounds. The figure for roller process was 5,394,000 pounds. These are rough figures. The figure for cheese was 5,639,000 pounds. Eggs, frozen whole, owned by the board totalled 3,194,000 pounds. Grade A large oiled eggs totalled 59,965 cases and eviscerated fowl totalled
831,000	pounds. These are the stocks which we hold at the present time.
I was asking for a comparison with the year before if they were similarly supported a year ago.
Unfortunately we do not have those figures here. As it happens, these figures just go back to March 11.
That is satisfactory. I will put a question on the order paper.

Can the minister tell us the names of the members of the advisory committee, how often the advisory committee has met and what is their remuneration or what expenses of members of the committee are paid?

Unfortunately I have not got a list of names here but I think we can reconstruct it quite readily. The members are Mr. Dewar from Prince Edward Island, Mr. Lutes from New Brunswick, Mr. Lemoine and Mr. Ferron from the province of Quebec, Mr. McCague and Mr. Hill from Ontario, Mr. McAllister from Manitoba, Mr. Turnbull from Saskatchewan, Mr. Don McKinnon from Alberta and Mr. Ellison from British Columbia.
Can the minister say what these people are paid for the time they spend at meetings and how many meetings of the advisory board have been held?

There has been a change recently in this regard and I was trying to get it straight in my mind. The members 
of the board were paid $35 a day for expenses plus their transportation expenses. They represented that they did not find this sufficient to cover their expenses and it has now been changed to $35 a day plus their expenses.

I am sure no one in the committee has any objection at all to the amount that the minister has stated is being paid to the members or the committee. Can the minister say how many meetings have been held and how many days have been occupied in sessions of the board.
Two meetings of the board have been held so far lasting two to three days each. Another meeting of the board will be held on the sixth of this month.
Can the minister say when the first meeting was held?
It was convened, I believe, on the fourth of March.

Mr. Chairman, this is certainly a very important act we are discussing. It is the whole basis of support for the agricultural industry with the exception of the initial prices that are provided under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. The support prices or floor prices now being paid represent the government's action toward implementing its election promises. In parliament and outside parliament the Conservative party has advocated adequate parity prices for many years. The Prime Minister has referred many times to two motions he moved in the house when he was in opposition calling for parity prices. Therefore the support prices under this legislation, and there are quite a number of them, are the government's answer to the promises it made to the Canadian people.
In the act passed last year a number of references were made to the cost of production and it was provided that in establishing support prices under the legislation consideration had to be given to the cost of production. As a matter of fact, prices were to be based on the cost of production. I should like to know what studies have been made in the department to determine the cost of production and what the minister might say is the cost of production for some of the important commodities that have support prices under this act.
There is a feeling amongst farm organizations and there is a belief amongst some of the members of the advisory committee which the minister just named that there is little or no regard to the cost of production in establishing prices under this act. I think that producers in the main would agree with

me when I say that those prices are not satisfactory prices to the producers in that, generally speaking, they are not sufficiently high to cover the cost of production and to give the farmer a fair return on his investment and his labour. I am very much interested in finding out from the minister how the board is guided by the cost of production, what figures are used and what studies have been made to determine the cost of production of those various commodities.

In connection with the first statement which was made by the hon. member as to parity prices, I should like to draw to his attention and to that of all the other hon. members of this committee that when his bill was under discussion last year I never used the term "parity prices" except to comment on the remarks made by the hon. member and other members of his party and of the Social Credit party in the house. At that time when I introduced the measure I made it very clear in every speech I made in connection with this matter, both in the house and during the election campaign, that I had deliberately avoided the United States system of support prices on the basis of what are known as parity prices. Over and over again I emphasized the fact that in my opinion and also in that of a large number of United States farmers the United States parity price system had proved to be one of the most colossal failures in history and that we were not going to introduce in Canada any system of that kind. I therefore do not think that the hon. member should say that I or others represented that this was a parity price system.
I said that the Prime Minister promised parity prices.

The hon. member knows that we fought the election as far as his part of the country was concerned, as he did, on the farm stabilization bill. He also knows what the results were. Certainly there was no question that we were introducing a parity price system such as that which exists in the United States and which most people have in mind when they talk about parity prices. There was never any suggestion of it.
As far as the cost of production is concerned in determining what these prices shall be, I think everybody knows that this is a fact. The determination of the cost of production as far as any particular commodity is concerned is an extremely difficult matter. First of all, I had better say this. Some studies in this connection are going on in the economics division of the department. In all cases we have attempted to take the cost of production into consideration and to relate
Supply-Agriculture
the price set to the cost of production. But I must say that the amount of definite and precise information available as to what the cost of production is for most commodities is limited. That is not true for all commodities but for most commodities the information available is sketchy. What we have done is to take the cost of production figures which have been supplied by producers of the different commodities and we have examined those figures and we have applied certain tests to them. As a result, we have tried to arrive at a reasonable cost of production figure.
Just a short while ago there was a little discussion between myself and the hon. member for Kootenay West with regard to the cost of production figures which were submitted by the fruit growers of British Columbia. This is just one example of the extreme diversity of opinion which exists as to what the cost of production of any particular commodity is. But I can assure the hon. member that we have made an effort to determine the cost of production of these various commodities and to relate the support price set to that cost of production.

I wonder whether the minister could say what the estimated average cost of production of any one of these commodities happens to be. The minister knows that section 2 of the act, subsection 2, says that in prescribing a percentage of the base price, and so on, the governor in council shall be guided by the estimated average cost of production of the commodity, and such other factors as the governor in council considers to be relevant. I think it is fair to ask what is the estimated average cost of production of the commodity which is written into the act and which by the act the governor in council is asked to consider in setting these support prices. There must be some means by which the minister has determined the estimated average cost of production. Nobody perhaps can prove that a given figure is precisely correct in every way but the act does not say that it must necessarily be foolproof; it must merely be the estimated average cost of production.

I have not the figures here in connection with that matter. However, there are one or two of them that run in my memory. I believe that the estimated cost of production of hogs here, we will say up to a month or so ago, was in the neighbourhood of $18 a hundred, live weight; and the estimated cost of production of Ontario wheat, it runs in my mind, was $33 to $34 an acre.

Can the minister say how the $18 figure was arrived at? Does it include labour? Does it include interest on the

Supply-Agriculture
farmer's investment? Does it include all of the cost of production figures in a normal accounting sense or is it merely an out-ofpocket cost figure which is a figure that the farmers themselves may sometimes use or consider when they are estimating their cost of production?

I cannot say precisely what all it includes. However, I know it includes things like taxes and interest on money invested and things along that line. I might say that that is the price for the production of hogs in Ontario. The biggest element in the cost of production of hogs, as the hon. member knows, is feed; and the cost of production in western Canada, of course, would be considerably less than that.
The figure was $18?
Yes.
When you have a support price of $25 a hundredweight at Toronto, I take it, what is the support price at Winnipeg or Regina or Edmonton?

That is one of the very matters which the advisory committee is going to discuss and make recommendations on in their meeting here on the sixth. We have not as yet said what the support prices would be at these various points because the price of hogs was well above and there was no chance within the last few months of this coming into effect. We have therefore delayed setting these levels until there could be another meeting of the advisory committee in order to get their advice in this regard.

I think the hog producers of this country would say that the minister's figures for the cost of production are far too low and that if you have an ordinary price differential between Toronto and Regina- a price differential which has prevailed many times in the past-of around $3 a hundred you would get a floor price of $15 a hundred-
Where do you get your $15?
The floor price is $25.

The minister said to me a while ago that in calculating his cost of production that figure was around $18 for Ontario and what I was trying to arrive at was that if the cost of production in Ontario was $18- and the minister now says it is much less in Saskatchewan-a comparable cost of production out there might be $18 less the difference in freight. I will admit that is a very rough way of trying to arrive at it-
A very, very rough way.

If the hon. member wants to bark he should stand up.
If the minister wants to give any other cost of production figure for Saskatchewan, well and good. He has the information and I have not, but I think that the hog producers will feel this cost of production figure is very low and that in fact it is a good deal lower than the hog producers would consider it should be. If the cost of production in Ontario is $18 and the floor price is $25, that means that the hog producer in Ontario could of course make a profit of $7 per hundred.
No, it is $18 live weight.
Live weight?

Yes, live weight, and as the hon. member knows hogs which are ordinarily 200 pounds will dress out at somewhere around 155, 156 or 157 pounds for a reasonable grade of hog, which means that the cost of production is approximately the same as the support price of $25.

That paints a much different picture. I think that is more nearly accurate if the minister is calculating on that basis. In other words, the support price is the cost of production and there is not included in it any real margin of profit. The minister has not yet told me whether it includes labour costs or not.

I think I did tell you that it includes taxes, interest on money invested and so forth and the deputy minister informs me it also includes labour costs. I do not have these figures here, as I say, and therefore I do not think it is very reasonable for me to try to answer in very great detail the questions put to me on this matter, which I think the hon. member will realize. I think I must say, however, that in regard to what he said about raising hogs in Saskatchewan I think I know a good deal more about the raising of hogs than does the hon. member. I have raised probably 10,000 to 20,000 more than he has. I have been in the hog raising business, off and on, for the greater part of my life and I am raising hogs at the present time. I have never at any time raised hogs when the margin of profit was as great as it is today. The hog-barley ratio is just about the best it has ever been in the history of hog raising in this country, and anybody who cannot make money raising hogs at the present time should not be in the hog raising business.
The minister has said that it is wonderful today, that it has never been better, but just about five minutes before he said it might drop $8 a hundredweight within the present year.
And it would still be profitable if it dropped that much.

In my opinion it would be most unprofitable from the standpoint of the producers who are trying to make a living to try to produce hogs at a floor price of $25 a hundredweight at Toronto. This is $2 per hundredweight better than the floor price Jimmy Gardiner used to have, and we complained bitterly that that floor price was too low. I am sure the hog producers in this country will feel that the floor price vhich is just $2 higher is not at all adequate.

If the hon. member will allow me I would like to point out to him that, as I have said, he is speaking about a subject about which I happen to know a great deal more than he does from personal experience and a floor price of $23 a hundredweight would still be much better than the floor price of $23 a hundredweight two, three, four or five years ago, because the price of feed is a good deal lower today than it was at that time and the biggest element in keeping hogs is the price of feed. That is your big cost factor. If you can get your hogs away in five months, for example, you will make more money than a man who takes six months to get them away and, on the other hand, if you get them away in six months you will make more money than the man who has to hold them for eight months. The matter of making money on hogs depends almost entirely on two factors; firstly, the cost of feed and, secondly, how well you feed your hogs and how fast you get them to market and therefore the amount of feed you put into them.

What the minister is saying is that the position for the hog producer is a little better now because when the farmer produces grain he can feed to the hogs he can make a profit because grain is not worth as much as it used to be. Of course that is exactly what we have been saying for many years, that the farmer's position has become worse.
We are doing something.
That is the whole point which concerns us-
We are doing a lot more about it than you could ever have done.

I would like to quote from the words of Mr. Olaf Turnbull, who is one of the members of this advisory committee. This quotation is taken from the Regina Leader-Post of July 9;
The Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act is designed to help the large operator and does nothing to prevent elimination of the family sized farm,
Supply-Agriculture
a member of the advisory committee to the board administering the act said Tuesday.
Olaf Turnbull told a meeting of the joint board of the interprovincial farm union council that the act aids the big operator and "lets the devil take the hindmost."
I think those are far stronger words than I have used tonight and this is a man who is in a position of authority. He is a member of the advisory board and he makes this statement about the act.
I am prepared to give the government and the minister any and every credit wherever there has been an increase in the support price to the extent that the floor price for hogs is higher-I give the minister credit for that-but I do submit that the floor prices under this act are not in keeping with the terms of the act itself at least so far as farm organizations have understood the act.
The farmers' union presented a brief to the government, I believe dated May 28, in which they complained that the cost of production was not considered as it should have been in establishing these prices. The minister has said that the election in western Canada was to some extent fought on the circumstances surrounding this act. That is true, but I would like to ask the minister when were the support prices established under this act and when was the announcement made as to the price levels under the act?

I think the first prices
announced under this act were on April 7. I could have announced some prices before that; at the time the act came into effect and was proclaimed on March 1. Had I announced the prices at that time my hon. friend would have gone around the country saying what he said in the House of Commons just before we adjourned, that the prices set under this act before the election were political prices, that they meant nothing but were just put in there for political purposes. I thought it would be better, therefore, not to set any prices before the election was over and thus avoid any controversy along that line. The prices I would have announced would have been these prices: 107 per cent, 110 per cent, 110 per cent, 107 per cent, 107 per cent, 84 per cent, 80 per cent and 110 per cent. These were the prices we had arrived at and could have announced immediately after the act was proclaimed and the stabilization through the advisory committee was first made on March 4, 5 and 6.
We could have announced those prices. The members of the advisory committee were very surprised that I did not announce the prices because those prices were all considerably above average for the 10 years which included what the farmer looks upon

Supply-Agriculture
as the best years he has had as far as prices are concerned, namely 1947 to 1950. Had I announced them, the hon. member would have complained ever since that I had announced them for political purposes and attributed the defeat of many of his colleagues to the fact we had put out those prices. I did not announce them because I did not want a lot of political controversy associated with these prices.

I do not know how the minister can have it both ways. He says the reason the other parties did not do so well was because of the support prices, and then he says the support prices were not announced until after the election. I made a statement during my campaign that as far as I was concerned the main commodities most people were producing would not have floor prices set above the market price, with perhaps the exception of butter, and I think that statement has been borne out. The government says it did no want to take advantage of other parties by announcing these prices in advance. This is a strange statement for the government to make when, as the minister has said, there are only four commodities whose prices are set a the moment above the market price. Certainly the floor prices on most commodities are below the market prices.
The minister has said he has never advocated parity prices. That may be true. The minister, perhaps, has never used that term-has never advocated it-but if the minister has not, certainly the Prime Minister has, and the Prime Minister has been very clear in this respect.
Would the hon. member give us his definition of a parity price?

I would think that the definition of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which is based on the period 1926 to 1929, would be an acceptable definition. They have had very excellent economists go into the whole theory of parity prices, and they have come up with that as a formula. Of course, if the Prime Minister were in the house I could ask him what a parity price is. Perhaps he will come down and grace us with his presence when we are talking about parity prices and the many promises he made during the election.
At Kipling on May 17, the Prime Minister is quoted in the Regina Leader-Post as follows: "By electing a Conservative government, he said, farmers would get parity prices." The Minister of Agriculture says no. In the Regina Leader-Post of May 18 the Prime Minister is again reported as saying:
[Mr. Harkness.l
"I urged this system of parity prices in 1941 in a resolution in the house . . . but every Liberal member voted against it."
The Canadian Press reported in the Ottawa Citizen of June 10, 1957, as follows:
He (The Prime Minister) promised that if a Conservative government is elected he will call a September session of parliament-
I believe he did that.
-to set up a system of floor prices for agricultural produce based on parity, cash advances for farm stored grain and a new loan scheme to aid young farmers.
So I think it is perfectly clear that while the Minister of Agriculture has not been known as a supporter of parity prices the position of the Prime Minister over the years is clear. He has been a complete advocate of parity prices. However, in the legislation we are now discussing there is no formula for the establishment of cost of production and with the exception of some very rough estimates on a few commodities neither the minister nor the board have adequate figures in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to speak on this item, but as a small hog producer and a new member of the House of Commons I must say I am greatly amazed at people in this house representing constituencies and trying to be, or being, spokesmen for agriculture and knowing as little about it as they appear to me to do.
The Minister of Agriculture definitely stated that he thought the cost of production of hogs was about $18 live weight. He definitely said "live weight". The hon. member for Assiniboia walked right into the trap. He does not know anything about hog production or prices. He does not know that a hog is sold on rail grade and that a good pig rail grades 75 per cent of live weight. And yet he wanted to be a good spokesman on the cost of raising pigs; he wanted to be the spokesman in this house for hog producers of western Canada. Yet he knows nothing whatsoever about hog producing.
Then the hon. member went on to read us what Mr. Turnbull had said about the present floor price on hogs. He said Mr. Turnbull had said it was only going to favour the large producers. I may add just as a point of interest that Mr. Turnbull himself is considered one of the largest producers of hogs in Saskatchewan.
Then he went on to say what the interprovincial farmers' union had to say about support prices on hogs. He said that on May 28 they said it was not high enough, and they still said it was not high enough. I met the interprovincial farm union on May 28. They said that the floor price was not high enough.

But what did they say about a month ago when they were down here? They said: Look out. We are going to have too many hogs.
They were contradicting themselves somewhere along the line, because you cannot have a floor price that is too low and still get too many hogs. I will point out that the supply of hogs is good this year. We have an abundance of hogs, and it must be remembered that as soon as you have a supply of something-particularly hogs-and I speak for the hog farmers, because I am one myself; a farmer is not going to produce something he is losing money on-or when there is an over supply they must be making their cost of production. As a farmer, I can tell you that you do not have to have a formula to know that when there is an overflow of something the farmer is getting cost of production out of it. I would advise the hon. member for Assiniboia, if he wants to speak on hogs, to begin raising some in his spare time and learn something about them.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to delay these proceedings beyond a few moments but I do ask the indulgence of this committee for a brief space of time in order to discuss a question which arises from this vote and which is of tremendous importance to western Canada.
Should I require some justiflcatian for taking these few moments I would remind the committee that the hon. members for Laurier and Bonavista - Twillingate took several hours of the time of this committee in this discussion to talk about the fate of one man. I would also remind the committee that the hon. members for Skeena and Assiniboia spent several hours this afternoon discussing cold storage plants.
Again I would remind the committee that the hon. member for Kootenay West treated us to a lengthy dissertation last evening with respect to a certain rooster and this evening he treated us to another dissertation with respect to prunes. May I also remind hon. members of the committee that we have had considerable discussion this evening with respect to hogs. Indeed, this might go down in history as hog night.
I wish to discuss a subject that vitally affects several thousand farm families in western Canada and surely in the light of what has taken place yesterday and today during the course of this discussion I am fully justified in doing so.
In referring to vote No. 43 I might point out that the hon. member for Lethbridge and myself are probably the only two hon. members of this house who can speak from experience and from a background concerning irrigation. We have a very intimate
Supply-Agriculture
knowledge of, not only the practice of irrigation, but the problems of irrigation and it is my hope that in the next few moments I may be able to say something with respect to those problems.
We have in southern Alberta approximately 500,000 acres now under irrigation and we have a potential of another 500,000 acres with the major irrigation works already constructed. I am not going to elaborate on this, other than to say that this area has many grave problems.
The province of Saskatchewan is on the verge of a tremendous irrigation development. Let me say at once to the Saskatchewan members on both sides of the house that there is no jealousy on the part of hon. members from Alberta with respect to this development. Surely after the promises of the last 25 years; surely after all the work that has been done in the engineering field and surely after the hope that continuously has been raised in the hearts of Saskatchewan farmers, they are definitely entitled to some development with respect to irrigation.
Let me assure hon. members from Saskatchewan that we in Alberta are extremely happy about the irrigation development now projected for the province of Saskatchewan, and we are especially delighted that coupled with it is a power development. Had we in Alberta a similar development, a similar coupling, had we the opportunity to join together power development and irrigation, we would be in a much happier position than we are today.
There is a feeling on the part of many people that if you build a dam, or otherwise impound water, and construct a canal, and from that canal have outlets to spread the water on the land you will immediately find yourself living in a land of milk and honey and all your problems will be over. I say this as an aside, but I have found that conviction in many places. I have found it on this side of the house and I have found it in the office across the hall from the office which I occupy.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and I have had many discussions with respect to the future of irrigation in Saskatchewan. He tells me quite spiritedly, that he has made eight or nine trips to the area in which I live, and he has seen the dahlias blooming, the trees budding and the vegetables growing, and he is convinced that when Saskatchewan has its irrigation development all will be well and life will be beautiful.
Let me say at once that irrigation has many problems. Perhaps sometime in the

Supply-Agriculture
future those of us who know something about irrigation from first hand experience will have an opportunity to outline those problems.
Suffice it tonight to say that the problems are twofold.
First of all there is the problem of the farmer. The irrigation farmer is confronted with a tremendous operating cost. In my own area, the Eastern Irrigation District, centring on the town of Brooks, in the province of Alberta, the farmers pay an annual water rate-that is a rate paid for the use of water-of $2.70 per acre. That is a cost of which the dry land farmer knows nothing.
Our farmers also pay an exceptionally high labour cost for the spreading of the water on the land. They are required to buy much more machinery than a dry land farmer with its attendant expense, and they are also required to pay much higher municipal taxes than apply in dry land areas, this for the reason that bridges must be constructed, roads wash out, and the incidentals of municipal operations in irrigated areas are much more costly than in dry land areas. Therefore, from the farmer's point of view, unless he has a highly-specialized cash crop his position is extremely risky.
In my area of southern Alberta, where at least 95 per cent of the irrigation in this country exists at the present time, the districts are very largely farmer-owned. In other words, other organizations that developed these areas in years past found them uneconomic. They found they lost money each year in their operations, and as an escape route turned the areas over to the farmers in those localities.
In so far as my own area is concerned, the Eastern Irrigation District, the Canadian Pacific railway after a very creditable development project, gave the district to the farmers, and also gave them $300,000 to operate it. The railway said, in effect, "We cannot make it go so you try it," and to the credit of the farm leaders in the Eastern Irrigation District, up to the present time, they have been reasonably successful. However, they have found it impossible in recent years, to lay away sufficient funds for the replacement of structures that will ultimately decay or become obsolete.
In our area, and this applies also to areas in the constituency of my friend the hon. member for Lethbridge, many of the structures are wearing out. They have reached the point in their existence when any day they may break or decay, and the farmers who are being served by those structures will find themselves without water.

What is the future of the replacement of these structures? We talk to our provincial government and receive very little encouragement. I presume that primarily it is a responsibility of the provincial government and yet, if the provincial government does not function in this respect many millions of dollars of farm investment in terms of land development, and farm buildings, will be rendered almost useless because, after all, we do operate in a dry area in the Palliser triangle and there will be a great amount of disaster.
The great need of these irrigation districts, of course, in order to obtain sufficient revenue with which to build up reserves for the replacement of these structures, is industries. We in the Eastern Irrigation District have very few industries. Today we have one sugar beet factory at Taber and my friend the hon. member for Lethbridge has two in his constituency. We are supplying only a very small percentage of the sugar consumed in the Canadian market, yet we are told that that is the limit. We cannot think in terms of sugar beet area expansion. We have, it is true, a few small canneries covering from 100 to 150 acres. We have in our district one dehydration plant and I understand we are to have two. But these small industries add very little in terms of total acreage. What the irrigation districts need are industries, the requirements for which will reach back to a majority of farms in the irrigation districts. Until we are in the position in the older and newer irrigation districts, of being able to establish industries for the processing of the specialized crops grown on irrigated land we shall continually be faced with a serious problem.
You may ask yourself, Mr. Chairman, what is the point of all these remarks?
The point is simply that we have in southern Alberta an experience of some 50 years in irrigation. We have in southern Alberta now a second and, in some cases, a third generation of farmers on irrigated farms. It is stated that it takes three generations of irrigationists to make successful irrigation farm operators. Certainly, a dry land farmer moving to an irrigated farm is a lost soul, and usually leaves the farm in that same state of mind. It is our hope-and I speak now, I think, for all the southern Alberta members-that under vote 43 the experience of our errors-and errors have been committed; there have been many of them, and most of them were committed by the government to which the hon. gentlemen opposite owe allegiance; I refer to nothing specific-yet the experience of the past, regardless of who was responsible for it, may

be consolidated, may be reviewed and may be applied to the benefit of the new area, the area in which we are all interested today, namely the new area in central Saskatchewan.

Item agreed to.
Experimental farms service-
Branch experimental farms, substations and illustration stations-
522. Construction or acquisition of buildings, -works, land and equipment-further amount required, $240,000.

I happened to miss this item on the main estimate because I did not expect the squall that was going on to pass so quickly. However, I just wish to say a few words on this item because it is of serious importance to a number of my constituents. The minister knows that throughout the years there have been repeated requests from,
I think, all of the provinces of Canada for the extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to all the provinces, to make it dominion-wide, and we in this group supported those requests over the years, as other hon. members have done, including the minister when he was in opposition. I think he made some rather vehement speeches in that respect. We are still of the opinion that if this act were operative across Canada in general it would be to the great advantage of a large number of people, and it would present a great opportunity for its application and utilization.
The minister knows what I am referring to; I mentioned it last evening. I may say, Mr. Chairman, I was rather surprised to hear the member for Medicine Hat claiming for a few minutes last evening when he was speaking on these items and also this evening that I was speaking with respect to prunes. I think he mentioned them. Surely, he would not deny me the opportunity to give expression to the views of my constituents and I think he will also acknowledge the fact that I am not given to over-vocalization of my inner thoughts. I mention this because it is of serious importance to a number of my constituents.
As the minister knows, I wrote him some time ago with respect to surveys of an area in my district, namely the Slocan valley, which I referred to last night. I was very pleased with the minister's interest in the matter and his response. We are doing the best we can to get the provincial government to take up the matter with the federal government so that something can be done with respect to those very necessary surveys in the area before any development can be planned.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
As I said before, I think a great deal can be done in that respect as a result of cooperation between the federal and provincial governments and the people directly concerned. I can assure the minister that the people in this district would be only too willing to extend their co-operation and assist in every way possible in the development of this valley.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has recommended the introduction of a Canadian national conservation and rehabilitation act. I think there is a great deal of merit in the suggestion. Will the minister inform the committee whether the government is giving consideration to the introduction of legislation of that type, say, at the next session of parliament?

Mr. Chairman, as I have indicated on numerous occasions, we are studying the matter. Whether we will be able to bring in any legislation at the next session I am not yet in a position to say. I might point out, however, that I did not like to stop the hon. member, but this item we are discussing has to do with experimental farms service. I think he is on soil and water conservation.
I thought we were on item 532. I had my say, anyway.

Item agreed to.
532. Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage-further amount required, $375,000.
My remarks apply to this item.
Item agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, while the minister has been appearing before the veterans affairs committee, I am sure he would like to inform the committee of the whole about the progress of the department in recent months.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words. I might say I have been waiting all evening to have this opportunity but sometimes it amazes me to see how slowly estimates pass. Then, in the last few minutes a change took place and they passed

Supply-Veterans Affairs very quickly. Of course, we all know that the estimates of my hon. friend, the Minister of Agriculture, are very important and it is not surprising that they took considerable time. I also think that the veterans affairs estimates are most important as well but there is not the controversy over those estimates that we find in the other departments. This is understandable, because veterans affairs estimates have to do with benefits to our veterans in the way <5f pensions, war veterans allowances, hospitalization and the many other benefits. *
We have a great many individuals to deal with in the Department of Veterans Affairs and this is one feature of our department which I would like to emphasize. Our work is dealing mostly with individuals. We have, for instance, pensioners still living from the northwest rebellion of a good many years ago; we have the South African veterans; we have the veterans of world war I and we have the veterans of world war II. We are today a comparatively young nation and we are paying out a very large amount of money for benefits to those veterans.
As I said a moment ago, it does not surprise me that there is very little controversy in connection with veterans affairs.
As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River just mentioned, my department's estimates have already been before the standing committee on veterans affairs. The members of this committee have had the fullest opportunity to meet and question officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs and this has permitted, I am sure, a more detailed examination and discussion of the various items in the estimates and of my department's activities than is possible on the floor of the house. I am sure that this has been a great advantage to the members of the committee.
This has been the first session of the standing committee on veterans affairs and as the minister of that department I am very pleased with the work of the committee under the very able chairmanship, may I say, of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. Many of the members of the committee are new to the house and I have been impressed and gratified with the interest they have shown in the affairs of the department. I am also very pleased with the obvious good will that all members have shown in considering the various problems before the committee. This is bound to result in improvements in the legislation amending the veterans charter and subsequent legislation.
The department's budget for 1958-59, submitted in both main and supplementary estimates, including provision for loans, investments and advances, totals approximately


$308 million, an increase of some $17,600,000 over the appropriations for 1957-58. Of this increase approximately $15,600,000 represents increased payments of war veterans allowances and of pension for disability and death, both of these increases being due to legislative changes. Most of the balance of the increase will be found in the provision for the operation of hospitals and administration which is due to higher costs of hospitals and medical services.
Hon. members will recall that effective July 1, 1957 the basic rate for married recipients of war veterans allowance was increased by $18 per month and the maximum annual income ceiling for that class was increased from $1,440 to $1,620 and for those with single status from $840 to $960. Again, effective November 1, 1957 the ceilings on maximum income for both single and married recipients were increased by a further $120 per year and the maximum monthly rate for single recipients from $60 to $70. These amendments, which were only in effect for part of 1957-58, together with the normal increase in the cost of this benefit, account for the additional provision of $9 million for the fiscal year 1958-59.
The increase in the pension vote results from certain changes in the scale of pension awards which became effective July 1, 1957. The legislative amendments provided for an increase in the basic 100 per cent pension payable to a single person from $1,500 to $1,800, and in the case of a married pensioner from $2,040 to $2,400. These changes, together with some further and minor amendments to the Pension Act effective November 1, 1957, are the main factors contributing to the requested increase for 1958-59 of approximately $6,600,000.
Representations have been made to me on behalf of Newfoundland disability pensioners and it is interesting to observe that on April 1, 1949, when Canada took over the Newfoundland pension liability as it existed at the date of union there were 1,816 disability and dependent pensioners, with an estimated annual liability of $779,021. As of June 30, 1958, the corresponding figures are 2,079 and $1,638,356.
The suggestion has been made that these Newfoundland disability pensioners should be treated on exactly the same basis as Canadian pensioners, and with this I entirely agree. In other words, instead of having their British awards of pension supplemented their entire awards should be paid by Canada. While I have every sympathy for these representations and, as I said a moment ago, I agree with them, they necessitate a study of the problem as relating to Canadians domiciled in Canada prior to world war I and world war II who

served with the British or allied forces. Their basic awards are supplemented to Canadian rates during residence in Canada, and at the present time the entire subject is under review with the hope that it will be possible to find a solution which will be beneficial to both groups and acceptable to the governments involved.
I mentioned in my earlier remarks that there has been a general increase in the cost of hospitalization and medical services, and provision for the operation of this branch of my department for 1958-59 is some $2 million greater than for the previous year. The general level of treatment activity remains fairly constant but could increase with the advent of the various federal-provincial hospital plans. As I assured hon. members of the house in a recent statement as to the effect of these plans on the treatment of veterans, it is this government's policy that the operation of provincial plans will in no way adversely affect the rights and privileges for treatment to which any veteran is now entitled at the hands of the department.
I might explain to members of the house that the department's treatment requirements are provided for in roughly three ways. As you are aware, the department operates its own treatment institutions in many centres but in those locations where for various reasons it has not been considered desirable to construct departmental facilities arrangements have been made with certain hospitals for the priority use of a number of beds. In all other locations where there is no particular continuing load treatment is provided in any available general hospital at the expense of the department.
I might mention at this time that the department has for some time been studying the problem of the accommodation available for the treatment of veterans in the province of Newfoundland. This is a location where the department had arranged for the priority use [DOT]of a certain number of beds in existing hospitals, but in the light of our experience, particularly with respect to domiciliary care accommodation, we have felt that this whole question should be considered again and certain recommendations have been submitted to the treasury board which are currently under consideration.
Referring now to the department's hospital construction program, I should explain that the policy is to bring existing accommodation and services up to an acceptable modern standard. In accordance with this policy, there has been a gradual replacement of old and outmoded accommodation but for financial reasons the department has had to restrict its major construction projects so that
Supply-Veterans Affairs not more than two are under way at any one time. During 1958-59 the two major projects will be the replacement of outdated accommodation at Shaughnessy hospital, Vancouver, and at Westminster hospital, London.
There are in the estimates now presented certain increases and decreases in the amounts requested for various services when compared with those provided for the fiscal year 1957-58. In the aggregate, however, the totals of these variations tend to offset one another. In closing my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I might mention that the requested provision to meet the department's administrative services in general shows little increase over that for the previous fiscal year. This fact shows, I think, evidence of the careful supervision given tc that phase of the department's operation costs.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to commend the minister on the statement he has just made and to say how particularly grateful I am to hear the references he has made with respect to the veterans of Newfoundland.
The minister has rightly stated that whatever political lines are drawn, when it comes to the matter of discharging our obligations to our veterans those political lines disappear and we are always at one in wanting to do our very best for our war veterans and their dependants. It is only right that there should be very little controversy with respect to these estimates because they are merely a financial projection of a policy laid down by this parliament and concurred in by all political parties. Since we are at one with respect to the policy we cannot find much ground for disharmony with respect to the financial means of implementing that policy.
The minister referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs, of which I am very happy to be a member, and I would like to concur in what he said with respect to the interest shown in that committee, particularly on the part of members who have been on the committee for the first time this session. There again no political lines are drawn whatsoever and we all try to do our duty to the veterans and to their dependants, also keeping in mind our obligations to this parliament and the public at large. I would like to join with the minister m the tribute he paid to the chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, under whose able chairmanship we have I think achieved great harmony and progress.
The veterans legislation, as I said, was brought in in the first place by an all-party committee but it must of necessity be revised from time to time to bring it up to date

Supply-Veterans Affairs and in line with the changing times in which we live. I have listened to the figures mentioned by the minister with respect to Newfoundland pensioners and I am not sure if I got them correctly but I think he said in 1949 the number was around 1,816 and that this year it had risen to 2,179. That is a very small increase over a ten-year period and of course in considering that increase we must also consider that time passes quickly and that a number of young veterans of the second world war and of the Korean war are now feeling the results of that service and are perhaps getting to the stage when they feel they should apply for some assistance from the Canadian pensions commission on account of their disability. However, that increase of 360-odd is very small and I think it also reflects the special position in which the Newfoundland veteran finds himself as a result of the system and the procedure to which he is now subjected.
I was very glad to hear the minister say he felt that the pensions of Newfoundland veterans should be paid in full by the Canadian government, like those of other Canadian veterans, instead of first being paid by the British ministry of pensions and supplemented by the Canadian pension commission. I know the argument has been put forward that the Newfoundland veteran is in the same position as veterans who were domiciled in Canada and who served in the imperial forces but there is one very great distinction which I would like to bring to the attention of this house and that is that veterans who were domiciled in Canada and who of their own free will voluntarily bypassed the Canadian forces to return home and join the forces of another country are in a very different position from that of the Newfoundland veteran.
The Newfoundland veteran did not do that; he could not do it because Newfoundland was not at that time part of Canada. He had to serve either in the forces raised and supported by the Newfoundland government or else in the imperial forces of the United Kingdom and he had no opportunity to bypass the Canadian forces so he should not be penalized. I do think that a person who voluntarily adopts a country and settles in it and then when an emergency breaks out sees fit not to join forces which are going to fight to protect that country but goes and fights with the forces of another country, deliberately passes up the benefits which might accrue to those people who fought in the forces of his adopted country. I must again emphasize that the Newfoundland veteran did not do that and he could not do it for the simple reason that Newfoundland was


not part of Canada so he did the best thing he could do and joined the imperial forces. The terms of union recognized that fact and it is expressly stated that the Newfoundland veteran would be treated just as though he had served in the Canadian forces.
I have again gone into some detail over this matter because this question of being domiciled and putting a Newfoundland veteran into the same category as people who were domiciled in Canada but who left Canada to join the forces of another country is a quite incorrect picture of the situation. I am very grateful to the minister for his assurance that the problem is under consideration and to hear that the minister is of the opinion which he expressed earlier this evening. I am a bit disappointed that it was not possible to bring down legislation this session in order to correct this particular situation but I do hope it will not be delayed beyond another session.
The minister also mentioned that consideration was being given to the provision of a veterans hospital in Newfoundland and this is something which is very urgently needed. We have no veterans hospital, nor do we have sufficient hospital facilities to take care of our civilian needs. We fully understand the difficulties involved in the setting up of a separate hospital for veterans but I would like to bring to the attention of the minister the hospital facilities at Fort Pepperell and to ask him if he might consider the possibility of acquiring those facilities which may perhaps be available at an early date, and which may be acquired and utilized at a lower cost than would be involved in the construction of a separate building.
Before I sit down, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say one word about our merchant navy. I think every member will recognize that as a country Canada has not done justice to the veterans who served in the merchant navy and who supplied an essential service without which victory could not have been won and without which we could never have maintained our other forces overseas.
I have known many of these merchant navy veterans to die without getting the assistance they needed and which was provided to other veterans no more deserving than they were. I know now of countless merchant seamen who are crippled but who-cannot provide for their families and their children as they should like to do. That incapacity has resulted from the hardships and the dangers which they underwent during the war period.
I should also like to include in the merchant navy the unit of the rescue tug:

service which also played an extremely important part, particularly in Newfoundland and on the Atlantic seaboard. I hope the minister will take into consideration again the legislation which we brought down last year and which gave veterans of world war I entitlement to war veterans allowance if they had served 365 days prior to armistice day in England. I do not believe that we have developed there a sound basis for the awarding of these pensions. I think that the earlier basis, under which the pension was awarded if these people had served in a theatre of war, was much more satisfactory than what we have now. I still maintain that it is not logical to say that a member of the naval force who escorted troop ships across the Atlantic served in a theatre of war and then to say that the soldiers and the veterans in transports were not in a theatre of war. I think that position is most illogical. I hope that we shall see fit before too long to bring in legislation which will qualify anybody who crossed the ocean to England or to Britain, anybody who crossed the ocean on service outside of Canada, to be awarded a pension on the basis that he served in a theatre of war.
That is all I have to say, Mr. Chairman. There may be one or two points that I should like to raise later on because, although I was a member of the veterans affairs committee, it was not possible for me to attend every sitting as I was also a member of other committees sitting at the same time. Consequently, it was not possible to raise in the committee on veterans affairs all the questions one would like to raise. I hope I shall be able to do that later on when the estimates are under consideration?

Mr. Chairman, my remarks are going to be quite brief this evening. Having been a colleague of the minister on the veterans affairs committee since 1945, along with other members on the committee, I want to say that we were very much pleased when he was appointed minister. We know where his heart lies. We know that he will do all he can to assist the veterans' cause in Canada at this time. If anyone wants really to understand what the minister thinks, all he has to do is to read the minutes of the committee on veterans affairs since 1945. He will then know what the minister thinks about the many problems that are brought to the veterans affairs committee. We all know the minister's attitude towards these problems but our major function is to convince his colleagues that he is right when he is presenting some proposal on behalf of the Legion or other veterans' organizations in this country.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
In the minute or two at my disposal I want to express our sincere appreciation of the good work of the senior officials of the department in Ottawa and across the country. The officials of this department are recognized, I think, by all the members of this house as being officials who are particularly and unusually interested in the problems with which they are called upon to deal. I also want to say the same thing with respect to the Canadian pension commission.
I think the request of members of this house over a long period of years for a standing committee on veterans affairs was fully justified by the results of the first sittings of that standing committee this session. The committee contained an unsually large proportion of new members who naturally were not well acquainted with the various aspects of departmental administration and of the legislation concerning veterans. But in the short time that the committee has had to sit this session that situation is rapidly changing; and regardless of party, there is a growing appreciation of the administration of the department and also of the many complicated aspects of veterans' legislation. We had an excellent opportunity to hear from the officials of the department and to ask them any questions that came to our minds or to our attention.
Quite recently the Canadian Legion held its national convention in Edmonton. I was very much interested in reading the speech the minister made to that convention because I think it was a jolly good speech from his point of view. I hope he continues in that vein. In any event, that convention passed a great many important resolutions, a fact which indicates that the veterans and their dependants, branches and zone councils, provincial conventions and finally the national convention have been giving serious study to the many problems that have to be adjusted for all veterans to receive justice in this country in the days to come. Those representations will be made to the government, I presume, officially on some day very close to Remembrance Day. I urge that members of this house, particularly members of the committee, give close study to them when they receive copies of the representations made to the government. Knowing the minister as I do, I am quite sure that those representations will receive sympathetic consideration.
I am going to conclude in a minute or two, Mr. Chairman. However, may I say that I have become extremely optimistic in recent days as to the possibility of progressive legislation. Do you know, Mr. Chairman, that in 1919, under a Conservative government the doors on the washrooms in this building were

improperly hung. This government has been in power only about a year and that mistake was remedied this week as a result of representations from a good number of members of parliament who unfortunately had their noses bumped on many an occasion. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that that is an omen of what is going to happen with respect to veterans' legislation and other legislation in the days ahead. I always take these little straws in the wind, Mr. Chairman, as showing the direction in which the wind is blowing. I hope that is a good straw in the wind.
When we meet next session, Mr. Chairman, I hope we shall find in the speech from the throne a good number of amendments to the legislation which will indicate that this government is going to take some further steps to improve veterans' legislation on behalf of the veterans of this country and their dependents.
